title: Where our water comes from, and when it is safe to drink

summary.text: Almost all the water we use starts as rain. Some rain flows into rivers and lakes. Some soaks into the ground and fills the tiny gaps between grains of soil and rock. That is groundwater. Wells and borewells reach down to it. People store water in matkas, tanks, ponds and stepwells, and clean it before they drink it. Water that looks clear can still carry germs and dissolved salts, because both are too small to see.
summary.art: A cut-away picture: rain falling on a village and a city, water soaking into the ground between pebbles, a borewell pipe reaching down, a river flowing to a tank, and a child at a kitchen tap holding a glass of water.

intro.hook: Fill a glass from the tap and hold it up to the light. It looks like nothing but water. Where was this water last week? And is there anything else in it?
intro.text: Most children say the water comes from the tap. But a tap makes no water. It only lets out water that is already in the pipe. The pipe brings it from a tank, a well or a river, and those were filled by rain. In this unit you follow your water back to where it started. You also dry spoonfuls of clear water on a plate, to see what was hiding in them.
intro.art: A glass of water on a kitchen counter, with a dotted trail behind it going back through a pipe, a tank on the roof, a borewell, and up to a rain cloud.

outcomes: I can name where the water in my home comes from, such as a river, a lake, a well or a borewell, and how it reaches the tap.
I can say what rain does when it lands: it soaks in, runs off or dries up. I can show which ground lets it soak in.
I can explain groundwater, and why wells go dry when people pump faster than rain refills the ground.
I can describe ways people store water, from matkas and stepwells to overhead tanks, and explain why a matka keeps water cool.
I can explain why clear water is not always clean, and name ways to make water safe: settling, filtering, boiling and chlorine.
I can measure how much water my family uses in litres, and show it in a table and a bar chart.
I can explain the problems of too little water and of dirty water, and say who they hurt most.
I can explain that the water we use is very old and goes round and round. I can describe how satellites weigh groundwater, and how water was found on the Moon.

terms.meaning: The place where something comes from. A source of water is the place we get it from.
terms.example: A river, a lake, a well and a borewell are all sources of water.
terms.art: A map with a river, a lake and a well, each with an arrow pointing to a house.

terms.meaning: Water that falls from clouds. It is where almost all the fresh water we use begins.
terms.example: In the monsoon, rainwater fills ponds, lakes and wells.
terms.art: Big drops falling from a grey cloud onto a tin roof.

terms.meaning: Water with very little salt in it. People, plants and most land animals need fresh water to live.
terms.example: River water, lake water and rainwater are fresh. Sea water is salty, not fresh.
terms.art: A river glass and a sea glass side by side, the sea one with salt crystals.

terms.meaning: Water we can see on top of the land, in rivers, lakes, ponds and reservoirs.
terms.example: The Kaveri, Vembanad Lake in Kerala and your village pond are all surface water.
terms.art: A river winding past a lake and a pond, seen from above.

terms.meaning: A big lake made by people, usually by building a wall called a dam across a river. It stores water for a city or for farms.
terms.example: Many big cities get their water from reservoirs far away.
terms.art: A concrete dam holding back a large blue lake, with pipes leading away.

terms.meaning: Water hidden under the ground, in the tiny gaps between grains of soil, sand and rock. It is rain that soaked in.
terms.example: The water in a well or a borewell is groundwater.
terms.art: A cut-away of the ground with water filling the gaps between pebbles and sand grains.

terms.meaning: A layer of rock, sand or gravel under the ground that holds lots of groundwater, like a giant sponge.
terms.example: Many borewells in India are drilled down into an aquifer.
terms.art: A sandwich of layers under a field, one layer glowing blue and wet.

terms.meaning: A hole dug down into the ground until it reaches groundwater. Water seeps into it from the sides and the bottom.
terms.example: An old village well with a rope and a bucket.
terms.art: A round stone well with a bucket on a rope, water at the bottom.

terms.meaning: A deep, narrow hole drilled into the ground, with a pipe and a pump that bring up groundwater.
terms.example: Many homes and farms in India pump water from a borewell with an electric motor.
terms.art: A thin pipe going far down through rock layers to blue groundwater, a motor on top.

terms.meaning: To take in water, the way a sponge or soil does.
terms.example: Rain soaks into a field, but not into a cement road.
terms.art: A sponge and a patch of soil both drinking up water drops.

terms.meaning: Rainwater that flows away over the ground instead of soaking in.
terms.example: On a tarred road, rain runs off into the drain.
terms.art: Rain running across a road into a drain, arrows showing the flow.

terms.meaning: When liquid water slowly turns into water vapour, an invisible gas, and goes into the air.
terms.example: Wet clothes on a line dry because the water evaporates.
terms.art: Clothes on a line with faint wavy lines rising off them into the air.

terms.meaning: A clay pot for keeping drinking water. Clay has tiny holes, so a little water seeps out and evaporates, which cools the water inside. In Tamil it is called a mann paanai.
terms.example: In summer, many Indian homes keep a matka in a shady corner.
terms.art: A round red clay matka on a stand, its outside slightly damp.

terms.meaning: A deep well with stone stairs going down to the water. People walked down further as the water level fell in the dry season.
terms.example: Rani ki Vav in Patan, Gujarat, and Chand Baori in Abhaneri, Rajasthan, are famous stepwells.
terms.art: A huge stepwell seen from above, with zigzag stairs down to green water.

terms.meaning: A covered underground tank used in the Thar desert. Rain falling on a clean, sloping courtyard runs into it and is stored for months.
terms.example: A family in a desert village drinks tanka water all through the dry season.
terms.art: A round, domed tank in a sandy courtyard, the ground sloping gently towards it.

terms.meaning: A curved wall of earth built across a slope to hold back rainwater, so it has time to soak into the ground.
terms.example: Villagers in Alwar, Rajasthan, built many johads to refill their wells.
terms.art: A crescent-shaped mud bank holding a pool of rainwater on a dry hillside.

terms.meaning: When something mixes into water so completely that you cannot see it any more. It is still there.
terms.example: Stir salt or sugar into water and it dissolves.
terms.art: A spoon of salt going into a glass, then the glass looking clear.

terms.meaning: Living things far too small to see, such as bacteria and viruses. Some of them make people ill.
terms.example: Germs in dirty water can cause tummy illnesses such as cholera.
terms.art: A glass of water with a magnifier showing tiny rod-shaped germs inside.

terms.meaning: An illness caused by a germ that lives in water dirtied by human waste. It causes very bad diarrhoea and can kill quickly if not treated.
terms.example: In 1854, a doctor in London, John Snow, showed that cholera spread through water from one pump.
terms.art: An old street pump with a black handle, a map with dots around it.

terms.meaning: To make water clean and safe to drink.
terms.example: Boiling water, adding chlorine and using a water purifier are ways to purify water.
terms.art: A pot of water bubbling on a stove, steam rising.

terms.meaning: A chemical added in very small amounts to drinking water to kill germs. Bleaching powder, used to clean village wells, contains it.
terms.example: Water from a city treatment plant often has a slight swimming-pool smell from chlorine.
terms.art: A worker at a treatment plant adding a measured scoop to a big tank of water.

terms.meaning: The tiniest bit of something that is still that thing. A water molecule is two hydrogen atoms joined to one oxygen atom. Scientists write it H2O.
terms.example: One drop of water has more molecules than there are grains of sand on all of Earth's beaches.
terms.art: A big ball (oxygen) with two smaller balls (hydrogen) stuck on its top, like two ears on a head.

terms.meaning: A unit for measuring how much liquid something holds. A big water bottle often holds 1 litre.
terms.example: A bucket often holds about 15 litres.
terms.art: A 1-litre bottle next to a bucket, with '1 litre' and '15 litres' labels.

explanations.definition: Almost all the fresh water we use starts as rain. We take it from two places: water on the land, called surface water, and water under the ground, called groundwater.
explanations.description: Rain fills rivers, lakes and ponds. That is surface water, water we can see. Rain also soaks into the ground. That is groundwater, hidden water. Every home gets its water from one of these, or from both. A city usually pipes water from a river, a lake or a reservoir far away. A village often pumps groundwater from a well, a borewell or a handpump. Some homes buy water from a tanker, a truck that carries water. A few coastal cities, such as Chennai, also take salt out of sea water in big plants, but that costs a lot of electricity.
examples: Bengaluru gets most of its water from the Kaveri river, more than 100 kilometres away.
A farmhouse near Coimbatore may pump all its water from a borewell.
In summer, many families in big cities also buy water from tankers.
explanations.art: A map of India's water sources: a Himalayan river, a reservoir behind a dam, a village well, a borewell, a tanker truck and a desalination plant by the sea, each with a pipe to a house.
explanations.context: Where does the water in your tap really start? This card names all the places our water comes from.

explanations.concept: What rain does when it lands
explanations.definition: When rain lands, it soaks in, runs off, or evaporates. Which one happens depends mostly on the ground it lands on.
explanations.description: Rain can do three things. It can soak into the ground. It can run off, flowing over the ground into drains, streams and rivers. Or it can sit in a puddle and slowly evaporate, turning into invisible vapour in the air. What happens depends on the ground. Soil, sand, grass and forest floors have tiny gaps that water trickles into. Cement, tar, tiles and roofs have no gaps, so rain runs off. A forest is best of all. Leaves slow the rain, and roots make channels into the soil.
examples: Rain on a grassy field soaks in. Rain on a tarred road runs into the drain.
A city with roads and buildings everywhere floods quickly in heavy rain, because little water can soak in.
A puddle on a sunny day is gone by evening. Its water went into the air.
explanations.art: Three panels: rain soaking into a field, rain running off a road into a drain, and a puddle evaporating under the sun with wavy lines rising.
explanations.context: When rain falls on your street, where does it go? This card explains the three things rain can do, and why the ground matters.

explanations.concept: Groundwater: water hiding in the gaps
explanations.definition: Groundwater is rainwater that has soaked into the ground. It fills the tiny gaps between grains of soil, sand and rock.
explanations.description: Dig into wet sand at a beach, and the hole slowly fills with water. That water was hiding between the grains. Groundwater is like that, but under the whole land. It is not usually a big underground lake. It fills tiny gaps between grains of soil, sand and rock, like water in a sponge. A layer that holds a lot of groundwater is called an aquifer. A well or borewell is a hole that reaches down into this wet layer. Groundwater moves very slowly, sometimes only a few centimetres in a day. Some of the water in deep borewells fell as rain thousands of years ago.
examples: Dig a hole in wet sand at the beach. Water seeps in from the sides.
A well gets almost all its water from groundwater seeping in, not from rain falling straight into it.
Most drinking water in Indian villages is groundwater.
explanations.art: A cut-away of the ground under a village: soil, then sand, then gravel and rock, with blue water filling the gaps in the lower layers, and a well and a borewell reaching down into it.
explanations.context: Water hides under your feet. This card explains where it hides, and how wells and borewells reach it.

explanations.definition: City water is taken from a river, lake or groundwater, cleaned at a treatment plant, then pumped through pipes to homes. Overhead tanks let gravity push it down to the taps.
explanations.description: In most cities, water travels a long way. First it is taken from a river, a lake or a reservoir. Then it goes to a treatment plant, a place that cleans the water. There the water sits still in big tanks, so mud sinks. It is passed through beds of sand and gravel, which catch smaller bits. A tiny amount of chlorine is added to kill germs. Then pumps push the clean water through pipes under the roads. In many buildings, a motor lifts it to an overhead tank on the roof. From there, gravity pulls it down the pipes to your tap. In a village, a borewell pump may lift groundwater straight into a tank.
examples: The overhead tank on your roof uses gravity. Water flows down from it, so taps work even when the motor is off.
If a tap upstairs is weaker than one downstairs, it is because the water has less height to fall.
After the water is used, it goes down the drain, into sewers, and often back into a river.
explanations.art: A long picture-strip: river, intake pipe, treatment plant with settling tanks and sand filters, a pump, pipes under a road, an overhead tank on a building, and a tap.
explanations.context: Water comes out of the tap, but how did it get there? This card follows the water from a river to your kitchen.

explanations.definition: Storing water means keeping it safely for later. People store rain and groundwater in pots, tanks, ponds, wells and lakes behind dams.
explanations.description: Rain in most of India comes mainly in about four months of monsoon. People need water all twelve months. So for thousands of years, people have stored it. About 4,500 years ago, the Harappan city of Dholavira in Gujarat had huge stone reservoirs to hold rainwater. Mohenjo-daro had hundreds of brick wells. Villages built ponds and tanks, and cleaned out the mud together every year. In the Thar desert, families built tankas, covered underground tanks. In western India, people built stepwells, so they could walk down to the water as it fell lower in summer. Women paid for some of the grandest stepwells. Rani ki Vav in Patan was built by Queen Udayamati nearly 1,000 years ago. Today we also use overhead tanks, sumps, steel drums and giant reservoirs behind dams.
examples: A matka keeps a family's drinking water for the day.
Rani ki Vav is so beautiful that it is printed on India's 100 rupee note.
A village pond stores monsoon rain, and helps refill the wells around it.
explanations.art: Two halves: on the left a stepwell, a tanka and a village pond, and on the right an overhead tank, a steel drum and a big dam.
explanations.context: Rain comes for a few months, but we need water all year. This card is about how people have stored it, from 4,500 years ago to today.

explanations.concept: Why a matka keeps water cool
explanations.definition: A matka cools water because water seeps through its clay and evaporates from the outside. Evaporating water carries heat away.
explanations.description: Clay looks solid, but it is full of tiny holes. A little water slowly seeps through and wets the outside of the matka. That water evaporates into the air. To evaporate, water needs heat. It takes that heat from the pot and from the water inside. So the water inside gets cooler. It is the same reason you feel cold when you step out of a bath with wet skin. A matka works best in dry, breezy weather, because water evaporates faster in dry air. On a sticky, humid day it cools much less.
examples: Sweat cools your body the same way, as it evaporates off your skin.
A wet cloth wrapped round a steel bottle also cools the water inside.
A matka in a breezy spot cools better than one in a closed cupboard.
explanations.art: A matka cut in half: water inside, tiny channels through the clay, little drops on the outside turning into wavy vapour lines, with red heat arrows leaving the pot.
explanations.context: Matka water feels cool on a hot day, without any electricity. This card explains how a clay pot does it.

explanations.concept: Clear is not the same as clean
explanations.definition: Water that looks clear can still carry germs and dissolved substances that we cannot see. Clear water is not always safe water.
explanations.description: Water can carry three kinds of things. The first kind is bits you can see, like mud, leaves and sand. These make water cloudy. The second kind is germs, such as bacteria and viruses. They are far too small to see. Hundreds of bacteria could sit side by side across the full stop at the end of this sentence. The third kind is dissolved things, such as salt, or harmful substances like arsenic and too much fluoride. They mix in completely and vanish from sight. So a glass of water can look perfect, smell fine and taste sweet, and still make you ill. The only way to know is to test it, or to make it safe before drinking.
examples: Sea water looks clear, but it is full of dissolved salt.
In 1854 in London, people loved the clear, cold water from one pump. It was spreading cholera.
In some villages, clear groundwater carries arsenic or too much fluoride that nobody can see.
explanations.art: A glass of clear water with three zoom bubbles: mud bits (crossed out because the water is clear), tiny germs, and dissolved salt particles shown as dots between water molecules.
explanations.context: Water that looks clear must be clean. Is that true? This card explains three kinds of things water can carry, and why two of them are invisible.

explanations.definition: Settling and filtering remove bits you can see. Boiling, chlorine and strong sunlight kill germs. Special filters are needed to remove dissolved substances like salt or arsenic.
explanations.description: Different dirt needs different cleaning. Settling means leaving water still, so heavy bits sink to the bottom. Filtering means passing water through cloth, sand or a filter that catches bits. Neither of these reliably removes germs. Boiling water until big bubbles roll, and keeping it boiling for a minute or more, kills germs. Chlorine kills germs too. Even strong sunlight can kill many germs in a clear bottle left in full sun for about six hours. Scientists in Switzerland tested this, and the World Health Organization accepts it. Boiling does not remove salt, arsenic or fluoride. To take those out, people need special filters, or a purifier called reverse osmosis, RO for short. Many RO machines also throw away a lot of water as they work.
examples: Many Indian families boil their drinking water, or use a filter or purifier.
City treatment plants settle, filter and add chlorine.
Boiling sea water does not make it drinkable. The salt stays behind in the pot.
explanations.art: Four panels: a jug of muddy water settling, a cloth filter over a glass, a pot boiling with big bubbles, and a clear bottle lying in the sun on a tin roof.
explanations.context: There are many ways to clean water. This card explains which way removes which kind of dirt, and what boiling cannot remove.

explanations.concept: How much water a home uses
explanations.definition: A home's water use is measured in litres for each person each day. Bathing, flushing and washing use far more water than drinking.
explanations.description: Most of a home's water is not for drinking. Each person drinks only about 2 or 3 litres a day. Far more goes on bathing, flushing toilets, washing clothes and dishes, and cleaning floors. India's planners say a city home with drains needs about 135 litres for each person, each day. India's Jal Jeevan Mission, started in 2019, aims to give every village home a tap with at least 55 litres for each person each day. Some families use far more than this, and some manage on far less. A dripping tap can waste many litres a day without anybody noticing. You can find out your own family's number by counting.
examples: One bucket bath uses about 15 litres. A long shower can use 50 litres or more.
An old toilet flush can use 10 litres. Many newer toilets have a half-flush button.
Washing a car with a running hose can use more than 100 litres.
explanations.art: A bar chart drawn on a kitchen wall, with little pictures: a bucket, a toilet, a washing machine, a cooking pot and a glass, the glass bar tiny.
explanations.context: How much water does your family use in one day? This card explains where most of it goes. Here are made-up results from a family water count, like the one in this unit.

chart.title: Made-up example: one family's water in one day
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a family water count can look like. Your family's numbers will be different.

explanations.definition: Water becomes short when rain is low, or when people take water out faster than rain refills it.
explanations.description: Rain in India is very uneven. Mawsynram in Meghalaya gets nearly 12 metres of rain in a year, taller than a three-storey house. Parts of the Thar desert in Rajasthan get about 20 centimetres, about the length of a pencil. Rain also comes in a few months, not all year. And there is a second problem. India pumps up more groundwater than any other country in the world. In many places, people pump it out faster than rain soaks back in. Then the water level falls, and wells and borewells go dry. In 2019, Chennai's main lakes almost dried up. Trains had to carry water to the city from Jolarpettai, more than 200 kilometres away. When water is short, the poorest families, and the women and girls who fetch water, suffer first.
examples: A village borewell that once struck water at 30 metres may now need to go down 100 metres or more.
In the summer of 2019, special trains carried millions of litres of water to Chennai.
Paving over fields and filling in ponds means less rain soaks in to refill the ground.
explanations.art: A split scene: a lush green Meghalaya hillside in heavy rain, and a dry Thar village with a woman carrying pots, with a bar chart of rainfall between them.
explanations.context: Some places get too much rain, some far too little, and many are using up their hidden water. This card is about water shortages, and who they hurt most.

chart.title: About how much rain falls in a year (rounded)
chart.note: Long-term averages, rounded. Mawsynram's bar is far taller than all the others.

explanations.definition: The GRACE satellites measured tiny changes in Earth's gravity. These showed where underground water was being lost.
explanations.description: How can anyone know how much water is hidden underground? In 2002, the United States and Germany launched two satellites, nicknamed Tom and Jerry. They chased each other around the Earth, about 220 kilometres apart. Water is heavy, so it pulls with a tiny bit of gravity. When the satellites flew over a place with more water, its pull tugged the first satellite ahead a tiny bit, and the gap changed. The satellites measured changes far thinner than a hair. From this, scientists worked out where water was being gained and lost. In 2009, a team led by Matthew Rodell showed that groundwater under north-west India, in Rajasthan, Punjab, Haryana and Delhi, was being used up faster than rain refilled it.
examples: New twin satellites, launched in 2018, carry on the same job.
The satellites can feel a whole region's groundwater getting lighter, year after year.
explanations.art: Two small satellites, one behind the other, orbiting above India, with a faint blue glow under Punjab and Rajasthan fading year by year.
explanations.context: Nobody can see groundwater from above. This card is about two satellites that measured it by weighing it with gravity.

explanations.concept: Why is there arsenic in some well water?
explanations.description: In the early 1980s, doctors in Kolkata saw patients with dark spots and hard patches on their skin. A skin doctor, K. C. Saha, traced the cause to arsenic, a poison, in their tubewell water. Since then, arsenic has been found in groundwater in West Bengal, Bangladesh, Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Assam and other places. Dipankar Chakraborti, a scientist at Jadavpur University in Kolkata, spent decades testing tens of thousands of wells. Scientists agree the arsenic was not poured in by people. It comes naturally from mud washed down from the Himalayas long ago. The harder question is why it gets into the water, and whether pumping makes it worse.
examples: Arsenic has no colour, taste or smell. Only a test can find it.
After testing, many tubewells are painted green if the water is safe and red if it is not.

perspectives.explanation: The arsenic sits stuck to tiny grains of rust in the mud. Living things too small to see, called microbes, eat parts of the mud where there is no air. As they do this, the rust breaks down and lets the arsenic go into the water.

perspectives.who: Charles Harvey and others, in a study in Bangladesh published in 2002
perspectives.explanation: Pumping huge amounts of groundwater for farms pulls new water and food for the microbes down into the ground. So pumping may be making more arsenic come loose.
Pumping matters in some places but not others. The arsenic in many wells was released long before pumps arrived. The full answer is different from village to village, and is still being studied.

explanations.art: A cut-away of river mud under a Bengal village, with tiny arsenic dots stuck to grains, some coming loose into the water around a tubewell pipe.
explanations.context: Some clear, clean-looking well water carries an invisible poison called arsenic. This card is about where it comes from, which scientists still argue about.

explanations.concept: What a water molecule is, and why water dissolves so much
explanations.definition: A water molecule is two hydrogen atoms joined to one oxygen atom. Its ends carry tiny electric charges, so it pulls many other substances apart and dissolves them.
explanations.description: Zoom in to a drop of water, far past any microscope, and you reach molecules. Each one is one oxygen atom with two hydrogen atoms stuck on, like a head with two ears. Scientists write it H2O. The oxygen end has a tiny negative electric charge. The hydrogen ends have a tiny positive charge. Opposite charges attract. So water molecules attract the tiny charged parts of salt, sugar and many other things, and pull them apart. Those parts spread out between the water molecules and can no longer be seen. This is why water dissolves so many things. It is also why water is so hard to keep clean.
examples: Stir salt into water. Water molecules pull the salt apart, and it disappears.
Oil does not dissolve in water, because oil molecules have no charged ends for water to pull on.
explanations.art: A zoom in four steps: a glass of salty water, a drop, water molecules shaped like heads with two ears, and those molecules crowding round tiny salt bits and pulling them apart.
explanations.context: Why can salt vanish into water, but oil can't? This card zooms in to the tiny molecules that water is made of.

explanations.concept: Your water is very, very old
explanations.description: Water does not get used up. It goes round and round. Rain falls, flows, soaks in, is drunk, is breathed out, evaporates and falls again. So the water in your glass has been in clouds, seas, rivers, plants and animals before you. Go back further. The hydrogen atoms in water were made in the Big Bang, about 13.8 billion years ago, when the universe began. The oxygen atoms were made inside stars. In 2014, a team led by Ilsedore Cleeves worked out something surprising. Up to half of the water on Earth may be older than the Sun itself. It may have formed as ice in a cold cloud of gas and dust, before our Sun was born.
examples: The water in your glass may once have been in a dinosaur, a cloud over the ocean, and a mango tree.
When you breathe on a cold mirror, the mist is water leaving your body to start a new journey.

perspectives.explanation: It is settled that hydrogen was made in the Big Bang and oxygen in stars. It is also settled that water goes round and round on Earth.

perspectives.who: Scientists, about water older than the Sun
perspectives.explanation: This comes from computer models of how water forms in space. It is a strong idea, but not yet proved.

explanations.art: A glass of water with a swirl behind it going back through a dinosaur, a cloud, a star and a dark cloud of space dust.
explanations.context: Is the water you drink new? This card follows it back, far beyond the tap, to the stars and the beginning of the universe.

explanations.concept: Where did Earth's water come from?
explanations.description: Earth has a lot of water. It covers about 70 out of every 100 parts of the planet's surface. But nobody knows for sure where it came from. Scientists can test ideas by looking at a rare, heavier kind of hydrogen in water. Water from different places in space has different amounts of it, like a fingerprint. So scientists compare the fingerprint of Earth's oceans with water from comets, asteroids and old rocks.
examples: In 2014, a spacecraft called Rosetta reached a comet. Its water had a different fingerprint from Earth's oceans.
Some meteorites, rocks that fall from space, contain water locked inside them.

perspectives.explanation: Icy comets crashed into the young Earth and brought water. But the Rosetta comet's water did not match, so comets may have brought only a small part.
Rocky asteroids from further out in the solar system brought most of it. Some meteorites from them have water that matches Earth's fingerprint well.

perspectives.who: Laurette Piani and her team, in 2020
perspectives.explanation: The rocks that built the Earth may have held enough water already. They studied rare meteorites like Earth's building blocks, and found enough hydrogen to fill the oceans several times.

explanations.art: A young, rocky Earth being hit by icy comets and asteroids, with a question mark over it.
explanations.context: Earth is the blue planet. But where did all that water come from? This card shows that scientists are still arguing.

explanations.definition: Water has been found on the Moon, on Mars and on several icy moons of Jupiter and Saturn, mostly as ice or locked in rock.
explanations.description: Water is not only on Earth. In 2009, scientists studying data from India's first Moon mission, Chandrayaan-1, found a thin trace of water on the Moon's surface. It was in the dust, not in lakes. Dark craters near the Moon's poles, where sunlight never reaches, hold ice. Mars has ice at its poles and under its ground. Far out in the solar system, Jupiter's moon Europa and Saturn's moon Enceladus seem to have huge oceans under thick shells of ice. In 2005, a spacecraft called Cassini saw jets of water spraying out of Enceladus into space. Wherever there is liquid water, scientists ask a big question. Could something live there?
examples: India's Chandrayaan-1 carried an instrument made by NASA, the American space agency. It found signs of water in the Moon's dust.
Enceladus sprays water into space from cracks near its south pole.
explanations.art: The Moon with icy craters at its pole, Mars with white ice caps, and Enceladus spraying a fountain of water into space.
explanations.context: Is there water anywhere other than Earth? This card is about water on the Moon, Mars and icy moons far away.

explanations.definition: More than half of the human body is water. The kidneys clean the body's fluids every day.
explanations.description: Every living thing needs water. More than half of your body weight is water. A newborn baby is about three-quarters water. Your blood is mostly water. It carries food and oxygen to every part of you. You lose water every day when you breathe out, sweat and go to the toilet. So you must drink to replace it. Your two kidneys are your body's own water-cleaning plant. Each day an adult's kidneys clean about 180 litres of fluid. That is about 12 buckets of 15 litres. They keep most of it, and send out the waste as urine.
examples: Breathe onto a cold steel plate. The mist is water from inside you.
When you are thirsty, your body is telling you it needs water back.
A cactus lives where rain may not come for months. They store water in their thick, fleshy stem, so they can keep living through the dry months.
explanations.art: A child's outline filled mostly with blue water, with two bean-shaped kidneys glowing like tiny cleaning plants.
explanations.context: Water is not only around us. It is inside us too. This card is about how much of you is water, and how your body cleans it.

agreed.text: Almost all the fresh water people use begins as rain.
agreed.evidence: River levels, lake levels and well levels all rise after the monsoon and fall in the dry months. Weather stations across India measure the rain every day.

agreed.text: Groundwater is rain that soaked into the ground. It fills the gaps in soil and rock, and it refills slowly.
agreed.evidence: Wells rise after rain soaks in. Scientists measure water levels in thousands of wells across India. Satellites that weigh water with gravity show groundwater falling where too much is pumped.

agreed.text: Germs in dirty water cause illnesses such as cholera and typhoid.
agreed.evidence: In 1854, John Snow showed that people who drank from one London pump fell ill with cholera. Later, scientists saw the cholera germ under the microscope. Cities that cleaned their water saw these illnesses drop.

agreed.text: Boiling kills germs, but it does not remove dissolved substances like salt or arsenic.
agreed.evidence: Boil salty water until it dries up. The salt stays in the pot. Tests on boiled well water still find the arsenic.

agreed.text: Water goes round and round. It is not destroyed, only moved and changed.
agreed.evidence: Water that evaporates from a plate in the sun is not lost. It is in the air as vapour, and it comes down again as rain or dew.

challenging.claim: Water that is clear, cold and tastes good is safe to drink.
challenging.who: Most people, most of the time
challenging.for: Dirty-looking or smelly water is often unsafe. So it feels sensible to trust clear, sweet water.
challenging.against: Germs and dissolved poisons are invisible. In 1854, London's favourite pump, known for its sweet water, spread cholera. Clear groundwater in parts of Bengal carries arsenic.
challenging.context: This card is about a common way of judging water: by how it looks and tastes.

challenging.claim: Illnesses like cholera come from bad smells in the air.
challenging.who: Most doctors in Europe in the 1850s. They called the bad air 'miasma'.
challenging.for: Cholera struck poor, crowded, smelly parts of cities most. People did not yet know about germs.
challenging.against: John Snow showed that cholera followed the water, not the smell. A widow far away in Hampstead, where the air was fresh, died after drinking water from the Broad Street pump. The same year, Filippo Pacini in Italy saw the cholera germ under a microscope.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea of where illness came from, and how it was overturned.

challenging.claim: A well gets its water from rain falling into it, or from an underground river.
challenging.who: A common picture in many people's minds
challenging.for: Wells rise after rain. And some caves really do have underground streams.
challenging.against: Very little rain falls straight into a well. Almost all well water seeps in from groundwater, which fills tiny gaps in soil and rock all around. Underground rivers are found in some limestone caves, but most groundwater is not a river.
challenging.context: Where does a well's water really come from? This card looks at a common picture that is mostly wrong.

challenging.claim: Water is the 'universal solvent': it dissolves everything.
challenging.for: Water dissolves more substances than almost any other liquid, such as salt, sugar, many gases and many rocks over time.
challenging.against: Water does not dissolve oil, wax, sand or plastic. Saying 'everything' goes too far. 'It dissolves a great many things' is true.
challenging.context: This card is about a famous phrase used for water, and whether it is accurate.

challenging.claim: Big dams are the best way to give everyone water.
challenging.who: Many engineers and governments, especially in the 20th century
challenging.for: Big dams store huge amounts of water for cities and farms, and make electricity. Many cities depend on them.
challenging.against: Big dams can flood villages and forests, and force thousands of families to move. People like Anupam Mishra and Rajendra Singh showed that many small ponds, tanks and johads built by villagers can also store rain and refill wells. Most experts now say both small and big ways are needed.
challenging.context: This card is about a real argument in India: big dams, or many small water stores?

challenging.claim: When John Snow had the pump handle taken off, the cholera stopped.
challenging.for: It is a great story, with one dramatic moment. The handle was taken off on 8 September 1854.
challenging.against: Deaths were already falling by then, partly because many people had fled the area. Snow himself said so. Removing the handle may have stopped a second wave. His real proof was his careful map and his count of who drank which water.
challenging.context: This card is about a famous story of how a deadly illness was stopped, and what really happened.

challenging.claim: Bottled water is always safer than water from a tap or a filter at home.
challenging.for: Sealed bottled water from a careful company is usually clean.
challenging.against: Some bottled water has been found unsafe in tests. Water boiled or purified properly at home is also safe. And millions of plastic bottles end up as rubbish in rivers and seas.
challenging.context: This card is about whether water from a bottle is always the safest choice.

big_questions.q: Who does the rain belong to? The person whose roof it falls on, the village, the river, or nobody?
big_questions.hint: Think about the groundwater under your home. Does it stop at the edge of your land?

big_questions.q: Should water be free for everyone?
big_questions.hint: If water is free, will people waste it? If people must pay, what happens to a family with no money?

big_questions.q: One family digs a very deep borewell and pumps all day. The neighbours' shallow wells go dry. Is that fair?
big_questions.hint: Remember the well in a jar. Whose water was the deep well really pulling up?

big_questions.q: A frog, a buffalo and a farmer all need the last water in a pond. Who should get it?
big_questions.hint: What would happen to the farmer's fields if all the frogs disappeared?

big_questions.q: The water in your glass may once have been in a dinosaur, a cloud and the sea. Does that change how you feel about it?
big_questions.hint: Is it your water, or are you just borrowing it for a while?

big_questions.q: Why can water look perfectly clean and still make you ill?
big_questions.hint: Think of salt stirred into water. Where did it go?

big_questions.q: If rain soaks into the ground so slowly, how long has the water in a deep borewell been waiting there?
big_questions.hint: Some water in deep borewells fell as rain thousands of years ago.

big_questions.q: How did people find water under the ground before there were machines and maps?
big_questions.hint: Look at which trees stay green in a dry summer. Where do termites build?

big_questions.q: Why do women and girls do most of the water-fetching in the world? Is that fair?
big_questions.hint: Who fills the water bottles in your home?

big_questions.q: Is there water on other worlds, and could anything live there?
big_questions.hint: Some icy moons may have oceans under their ice, in the dark.

big_questions.q: John Snow's map saved lives because he looked at where people got their water. What other problems could you solve by drawing a map?
big_questions.hint: Where do people slip? Where do mosquitoes breed? Where are the shady places?

story.title: The Sweetest Water in London
story.note: Real: the Broad Street pump and its famous water, the cholera outbreak of 1854, Mrs Susannah Eley in Hampstead who had the pump's water brought to her and died of cholera, her niece from Islington, the brewery workers and the workhouse with their own wells, Dr John Snow's questions and map, and the pump handle taken off on 8 September 1854. In real life, Snow learned about Mrs Eley from one of her sons. Tilly, the carter Mrs Pike, and their talk with Snow are made up.
text: In the summer of 1854, the best water in London came out of a pump on Broad Street. Everybody said so. It was cold even in August. It was as clear as a window. People walked past two other pumps just to fill their jugs there.

Tilly was nine, and that pump was her job. Every morning she pumped the long iron handle until a big stone bottle was full. She pushed the cork in tight and lifted the bottle onto Mrs Pike's cart. Then she rode beside Mrs Pike, out of the crowded streets and up the long green hill to Hampstead.

In Hampstead, in a quiet house with roses by the door, lived old Mrs Eley. Her sons ran a factory on Broad Street. She had moved away to the fresh air of the hill, but she would drink no water except Broad Street water. 'Hampstead water tastes of nothing,' she told Tilly, every single morning. 'Broad Street water tastes of something.' Then she gave her a biscuit.

At the end of August, a terrible illness came to Broad Street. It was called cholera. It came fast, with a burning thirst and a sickness of the stomach. Some people who were well at breakfast were dead by night. The church bell rang and rang. Families piled their chairs onto carts and fled.

The doctors said it came from bad air. Soho smelled of drains, horses and rubbish, and in those days most people thought illness floated in on a stink. Tilly's mother tied a cloth soaked in vinegar over her nose. 'Breathe through that,' she said, 'and don't you dare stop for anybody.'
So Tilly did not stop. She pumped the bottle full and rode up the hill, where the air smelled of roses and cut grass. Up there, nobody had cholera. Up there, Tilly felt safe.
On Thursday she left the bottle at Mrs Eley's door, as always. Mrs Eley's niece was visiting from Islington, and she waved at Tilly from the window with a glass in her hand.

On Saturday, the curtains of the house were closed. Mrs Pike took off her hat and spoke to the maid. When she climbed back onto the cart, her face was grey. 'Cholera,' she said quietly. 'Both of them. The old lady, and the niece.'

Tilly could not understand it. All the way down the hill, she kept thinking. The bad air of Soho could not have floated all the way up here. The wind had been blowing the other way all week. Nobody else on the hill was ill. What had travelled from Broad Street to that house with the roses?
Then she looked down at her feet. In the straw of the cart sat the empty stone bottle, the one she had filled on Thursday.
Tilly felt sick. She had carried that bottle herself, every single day.

That afternoon, Tilly saw a thin, serious man walking slowly along Broad Street. He had a notebook. He was knocking on doors, and at every door he asked the same strange question. 'Where did this family get its water?' People said he was Dr Snow, and that he was a bit odd. Everybody knew it was the air.
Tilly ran after him. Her words came out in a tumble: the bottle, the cart, the hill, the roses, the old lady, the niece with the glass at the window.

Dr Snow stopped writing. He looked at Tilly for a long moment. 'Hampstead,' he said. 'Fresh air, and no cholera. And the only thing from Broad Street in that house was the water.' He wrote it down very carefully. 'Do you know the brewery on this street?' he asked. 'Seventy men work there. Not one has fallen ill. They drink beer, and the brewery has its own well. The workhouse round the corner has hundreds of people and its own well too. Hardly any of them are sick.'
'But the pump water is the best in London,' said Tilly. 'Everyone says so. It's so clear.'

'Yes,' said Dr Snow. 'It is very clear.' He closed his notebook. 'Whatever is making people ill is far too small to see. So we cannot ask our eyes. We have to ask the water where it went, and who drank it.'
That evening, Dr Snow went to the men who looked after the parish. He showed them his notes. On 8 September, they agreed to take the handle off the Broad Street pump.

People grumbled. They had to walk further, to a pump whose water was warmer and tasted of nothing. The next morning, Tilly stood beside the pump with no handle. A small boy came along with an empty jug, frowning. She pointed him down the road to the other pump.
'That water doesn't taste nice,' he said.
'No,' said Tilly. 'It doesn't.' And she walked with him, carrying the jug.

Later, Dr Snow drew a map of the streets. He put a little black bar for each person who had died. The bars piled up thickly round the Broad Street pump, like iron filings round a magnet. A young priest called Henry Whitehead, who at first thought Snow was wrong, went from house to house checking. In the end he found that a sick baby's nappies had been washed into a leaking pit right next to the well.
Today, on that same street in London, there is a copy of the old pump. It has no handle.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the clue that cracks the mystery is distance. The cholera reached Mrs Eley's house on a hill with fresh air, where nobody else was ill, and the only thing from Broad Street in that house was the water. So the illness was not in the air. It was in water that looked, smelled and tasted perfect. Germs are too small to see, so clear water is not always clean water. The way to find danger was to trace where the water came from and who drank it. The story also quietly asks who gets remembered: the doctor with the map, the priest who changed his mind, or the people who carried the water.
ask: Why did people trust the Broad Street pump more than any other?
Mrs Eley lived far away, in fresh air, and nobody near her was ill. Why was that the big clue?
The brewery men and the workhouse people mostly stayed well. What did they have that the others did not?
Dr Snow said, 'We cannot ask our eyes.' What did he mean?
Henry Whitehead set out to prove Dr Snow wrong, and changed his mind. Have you ever changed your mind because of evidence?

games.title: Drop's Journey
games.players: 2 to 4 players, or one child playing against the app
games.context: This is a board game about where rain goes. Each player is a raindrop trying to reach the village well, by soaking into the ground and travelling as groundwater.

printables.title: A board of 30 squares, from the cloud to the well
items: 1 START: you fall from a cloud
2 You land on a forest floor. Soak in. Go forward 3.
3 A tarred road. You run off into a drain. Go back 2.
4 You trickle between sand grains.
5 A leaf catches you. Miss a turn.
6 Hot sun! You evaporate. Go back to START.
7 A grassy field. Soak in. Go forward 2.
8 A tin roof. You run into a gutter. Go back 3.
9 A johad, a mud wall, slows you down. Soak in. Go forward 3.
10 You seep down through gravel.
11 A tree root drinks you. Miss a turn.
12 A tiled courtyard. You run off. Go back 2.
13 A village pond. You sink in slowly. Go forward 1.
14 You rest in the gaps of the rock for a hundred years.
15 A borewell pumps too fast. Go back 2.
16 You slide sideways through an aquifer, a wet rock layer. Go forward 2.
17 A tanka catches you from a clean roof. Go forward 2.
18 You seep past a leaking sewer pipe and pick up germs. Go back 1.
19 Someone leaves a tap running. Back to START.
20 You join the groundwater.
21 You move only a few centimetres today. Groundwater is slow.
22 A farmer floods a field all afternoon. Go back 3.
23 You pick up some dissolved salt from the rock.
24 You trickle towards a deep stepwell.
25 A family fixes a dripping tap. Go forward 2.
26 You pass through a sand layer, which catches mud.
27 A cement building covers the ground above you.
28 Rain refills the ground behind you. Go forward 1.
29 You find a crack in the well wall.
30 WELL: you made it!

printables.title: One raindrop counter for each player
Where my drop went
items: Squares where I soaked in
Squares where I ran off
Squares where I evaporated
How many turns to reach the well

rules: Each player is a raindrop. Everyone starts at the cloud, on square 1.
Take turns to roll a dice and move.
Read your square out loud and do what it says.
Before you move again, say why the square sent you forward or back. For example, 'Cement has no gaps, so rain runs off.'
If a square sends you back to START, begin again at the cloud.
The first drop to reach the WELL wins. Then play again. Can anyone get there without being sent back?

flow.do: 1. Put the board in the middle. 2. Give each player a raindrop counter on square 1. 3. Have a dice ready.
flow.say: You are each a raindrop. You have just fallen out of a cloud. Your job is to reach the village well. But the well only gets water from under the ground.
flow.kid: You are a raindrop! You just fell from a cloud. Your goal is the village well. Put your drop on square 1.
flow.context: This is the first step of Drop's Journey. It is a board game where each player is a raindrop trying to reach a well.

flow.do: Play one practice turn together. Land on square 3, the tarred road.
flow.say: Let's practise. You landed on a tarred road. The square says go back 2. Why?
flow.kid: Practice turn. You land on a tarred road. Go back 2. Why do you think?

check.q: A raindrop lands on a tarred road. Why is that bad news for reaching the well?
options: The road has no gaps, so the drop runs off into a drain
The road soaks it up too fast
check.why: A tarred road has no gaps for water to trickle into. So the drop runs off into a drain, and it cannot soak down to the groundwater that fills the well. Picking 'soaks it up' usually means thinking all ground is like soil.

flow.do: 1. Take turns. 2. Each player reads their square aloud. 3. Before moving, they say why the square sends them forward or back. 4. Fill in the score sheet as you go.
flow.say: Remember to say why. Why does a forest help? Why does a tin roof send you back?
flow.kid: Roll and move. Read your square. Say why it helps or not. Then mark your score sheet.

ask.q: Why does a forest floor help a drop reach the well?
good: Leaves slow the rain down.
Soil and roots have gaps, so water soaks in.

ask.q: Why does the tanka square send you forward?
good: The tanka catches rain from a clean roof and stores it.
The water is kept, not lost.

flow.parent: Squares 3, 8 and 12 send drops back, because rain runs off hard ground. Squares 6, 19 and 22 send drops back through evaporation and waste. Squares 2, 7 and 9 help, because water soaks in. Square 15 shows over-pumping. Square 23 shows how water picks up dissolved salts from rock.

flow.do: When someone reaches the well, stop. Look at everyone's score sheets together.
flow.say: Look at your score sheet. Where did you soak in? Where did you run off? What kind of land helps a well stay full?
flow.kid: Look at your score sheet. Count your soak-in squares. Count your run-off squares. What helps the well most?
flow.think: If our whole street were cement, how would the well get water?

games.title: Drink, Boil or Never?
games.players: 2 to 5 players, or one child with the app
games.context: This is a card game about safe water. For each water card, players decide: can you drink it as it is, must you make it safe first, or should you never drink it at all?

printables.title: 20 water cards to cut out
items: A sealed bottle of water from a shop, with the seal unbroken
Water from a stream in the hills, clear and very cold
A puddle on the road after rain
Water from the sea at Marina beach
Water from your home purifier, working properly
Water from a village handpump that has never been tested
Water from a well that was tested and found to have arsenic
Rainwater caught in a clean steel bowl, left out for two days
Tap water in a hotel in a city you do not know
Water that was boiled well and cooled in a clean, covered pot
Muddy river water, left to settle, then poured through cloth
Water from a clean, covered matka, filled with boiled water
Water from a bucket with a dead insect in it
Water from a borewell where the test showed too much fluoride
Melted ice from a street-side ice block
Water from a clear bottle left in strong sun all day on a roof
Water from a garden hose lying in the sun
Water from a fish tank
Water from a stepwell where people also wash
Water from your own tap at home, from a city treatment plant

printables.title: Three mats
items: DRINK IT: safe as it is
MAKE IT SAFE FIRST: boil it, or purify it
NEVER DRINK IT

rules: Shuffle the 20 water cards. Put them face down in a pile.
On your turn, take a card and read it out loud.
Put it on one of the three mats: DRINK IT, MAKE IT SAFE FIRST, or NEVER DRINK IT.
Say why. A good reason wins one drop token.
Other players can challenge you. If they give a better reason, they win the token instead.
When the cards run out, the player with the most tokens wins.

flow.do: 1. Lay out the three mats. 2. Shuffle the 20 water cards and put them face down. 3. Put the drop tokens in a bowl.
flow.say: Every card is some water. For each one, we decide. Can we drink it as it is? Must we make it safe first? Or should we never drink it at all?
flow.kid: Lay out the three mats. Mix up the cards. For each water card, choose a mat. Drink it, make it safe first, or never.
flow.context: This is the first step of Drink, Boil or Never? It is a card game about deciding when water is safe to drink.

flow.do: Play a practice card together: 'Water from a stream in the hills, clear and very cold.'
flow.say: This stream water is clear and cold. Is it safe as it is?
flow.kid: Practice card: clear, cold stream water. Which mat? Tap your answer.

check.q: Water from a stream in the hills, clear and very cold. Which mat?
options: DRINK IT: it is clear and cold
MAKE IT SAFE FIRST: boil or purify it
check.why: Clear, cold water can still carry germs from animals or people upstream. Germs are far too small to see. Boiling it, or purifying it, makes it safe. Picking 'drink it' usually means trusting how water looks. That is exactly the mistake people made with the Broad Street pump.

flow.do: 1. Take turns drawing a card and placing it on a mat. 2. The player says why. 3. Others may challenge. 4. Give a drop token for each good reason.
flow.say: Remember, a good reason wins a token. Can anyone give a better reason?
flow.kid: Take a card. Put it on a mat. Say why. A good reason wins a 💧 token.

ask.q: Why can't we just boil the water from the well with arsenic?
good: Boiling kills germs but does not take out arsenic.
The arsenic is dissolved. It stays in the pot.

flow.parent: Good placements. DRINK IT: the sealed bottle, the working purifier, the boiled and covered water, and the matka filled with boiled water. MAKE IT SAFE FIRST: the stream, the untested handpump and the hotel tap. Also the settled river water, the rainwater left out, the street ice and the stepwell. NEVER: the puddle, the sea water, the arsenic well, the fluoride borewell, the fish tank the bucket with the insect and the garden hose. Old water sits in a hose and in a fish tank, and germs grow in the old water. Boiling does not remove salt, arsenic or fluoride. City tap water depends on your city. Many families boil or purify it to be sure. The sunny bottle is tricky. Sunlight can kill many germs. But it needs a clean, clear bottle in strong sun for about six hours.

flow.do: Count the tokens. Then look at the NEVER mat together.
flow.say: Look at the NEVER pile. Which of these waters looked clear? Why can't boiling save them?
flow.kid: Count your tokens. Look at the NEVER pile. Which ones looked clear? Why can't we just boil them?
flow.think: If you can't see what is in water, how can anyone ever know it is safe?
