items.p: Where does almost all the fresh water we use begin?
items.why: Rain fills rivers, lakes and the ground. Taps and tanks only pass water on. Picking the tap or the tank means stopping the trail too early. The sea is salty, so we cannot drink it without removing the salt.
items.art: A rain cloud above a river, a lake and a well.

items.p: Water hidden under the ground, in the gaps between grains of soil and rock, is called ____.
items.why: Groundwater is rain that soaked into the ground. Wells and borewells pull it up.

items.p: In Rain on Four Grounds, you pour the same mug of water on a pot of soil, a tray of sand and a tile. Guess first: where will most of the water run off?
items.why: A tile has no gaps for water to go into, so the water runs off its edges. Sand and soil have gaps between their grains, so water soaks in. Sand soaks it up fastest, because its gaps are biggest.
items.context: This question is about Rain on Four Grounds, where you poured the same mug of 'rain' on different kinds of ground and watched where it went.

items.p: Sort these grounds. Does rain mostly soak in, or run off?
items: a grassy field
Soaks in
a tarred road
Runs off
a forest floor
Soaks in
a tin roof
Runs off
a sandy beach
Soaks in
a tiled courtyard
Runs off
items.a: see items
items.why: Soil, sand, grass and forest floors have gaps for water to trickle into. Roads, roofs and tiles have none.

items.p: Match each water source to what it is.
pairs: water flowing over the land towards the sea
a deep, narrow hole with a pump that brings up groundwater
a big lake made by building a dam across a river
a truck that carries water to homes
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These are the main places our water comes from. Rivers and reservoirs are surface water. Borewells bring up groundwater. Tankers carry water from somewhere else.

items.p: Most of the water in a well fell straight into it as rain.
items.why: False, though it is a common picture. Almost all of it seeps in from the groundwater around the well. That water soaked into the land, sometimes far away and long ago.

items.p: Why does water in a clay matka stay cool?
opts: Clay is made of something cold
The matka keeps the sunlight out
Water seeps through the clay and evaporates, taking heat away
The water inside slowly turns to ice
items.why: Evaporating water carries heat away, so the water inside cools. 'Clay is cold' is a common guess. But a dry clay pot left in the sun gets hot like anything else. Any covered pot keeps sunlight out, but that does not explain why a matka is cooler than a steel pot.

items.p: Old stepwells in India have long stone stairs going down to the water. Why were the stairs built?
opts: So people could reach the water even when its level fell in the dry season
Only to make the well look beautiful
items.why: In the dry months the groundwater level falls, and the water in the well sinks lower. The stairs let people walk down to it, however low it went. Many stepwells are also beautiful, but the stairs were built for reaching the water.

items.p: If water looks clear, it is always safe to drink.
items.why: False. Germs are too small to see. Salt, arsenic and fluoride can be dissolved in water and stay invisible. Clear water can still be unsafe.

items.p: Which way kills germs in water?
opts: Boiling it until big bubbles roll
Putting it in a steel tumbler
items.why: Boiling kills germs. Settling and a cloth remove bits you can see, but germs are far too small to be caught that way. Most slip right through the cloth.

items.p: A bucket holds about 15 litres. Kavitha uses 2 full buckets of water for her bath. She uses ____ litres.
items.why: 2 lots of 15 litres is 15 + 15 = 30 litres. A litre is a unit for how much liquid something holds. A big water bottle often holds 1 litre.

items.p: In most homes, which job uses the least water each day?
items.why: Each person drinks only about 2 or 3 litres a day. Bathing, flushing and washing use far more. Many people guess drinking is a big one, because drinking is what we think of first.

items.p: Write the journey of the water in your home, from where it really begins to your tap. Use arrows between the steps.
items.a: Any journey with a real source and real steps. For example: rain filled the river → the river water went to a treatment plant → pipes took the water to our sump → the motor lifted it to the overhead tank → it came down to our tap.
items.why: A strong answer starts at a real source, such as a river, a lake or a borewell, and follows each step to the tap.
items.context: This question is about Follow the Pipe, where you traced your home's water backwards from the tap.

items.p: Anu, a girl in Class 2, says: 'Our water comes from the overhead tank, so we will never run out.' What has she missed?
items.a: The tank does not make water. It is filled by a motor from a sump, a borewell or the city pipe. If the river, the lake or the groundwater runs low, the tank stays empty too.
items.why: A strong answer follows the water back past the tank to its real source, and says that the source can run low.

items.p: Name two places in your home or street where you could catch or save rain. Say how.
items.a: Any two sensible ideas. For example: put a bucket under the drainpipe to water the plants, or leave a patch of soil unpaved so rain can soak in.
items.why: Catching rain from roofs, and leaving soil open so rain soaks in, both save water. A strong answer says how each idea would work.

items.p: Draw a well and the ground around it. Show where the groundwater is, and how it gets into the well.
items.a: The drawing shows water filling the gaps in soil or rock below the ground, with arrows showing it seeping into the well from the sides and the bottom.
items.why: Well water seeps in from the groundwater all around. Very little falls straight in as rain.
items.art: An empty cut-away outline of the ground with a well shape drawn in it.

items.p: Look at the chart from the Cool Matka Test. Which container kept the water coolest?
opts: The bottle in a wet cloth
items.why: The matka's bar is the shortest, at 24 °C. On this chart a shorter bar means cooler water. Picking the steel bottle usually means reading the tallest bar as the best.
items.context: This question is about the Cool Matka Test. You filled a clay matka, a steel bottle and a steel bottle wrapped in a wet cloth with the same water, and measured them after 4 hours in the shade.

chart.title: Made-up example results: water temperature after 4 hours in the shade

items.p: In the Cool Matka Test, all three started at 30 °C. After 4 hours, the matka water was 24 °C. It cooled by ____ degrees.
items.why: 30 take away 24 is 6. So the matka cooled the water by 6 degrees.
items.context: This question is about the Cool Matka Test. You filled a clay matka, a steel bottle and a steel bottle wrapped in a wet cloth with the same water, and measured them after 4 hours in the shade.

chart.title: Made-up example results: water temperature after 4 hours in the shade

items.p: On a hot, dry day the matka water is cool. On a sticky, humid day in the monsoon, it is hardly cooler than the room. Why?
opts: The clay gets wet from the rain
Water evaporates slowly when the air is already full of water vapour
items.why: The matka cools because water evaporates from its outside. Humid air already holds a lot of vapour, so evaporation is slow, and less heat is carried away. This is also why wet clothes dry slowly in the monsoon.
items.context: This question is about the Cool Matka Test. You filled a clay matka, a steel bottle and a steel bottle wrapped in a wet cloth with the same water, and measured them after 4 hours in the shade.

items.p: In the jar well, the water level fell after 10 pumps. Then you covered the soil with plastic and poured more rain on top. What happened?
opts: The level did not rise, because the rain could not soak in
items.why: The plastic stopped the rain soaking down, just like cement over real ground. So nothing refilled the groundwater. Picking 'rose a lot' means thinking rain reaches the well whatever covers the ground.
items.context: This question is about A Well in a Jar. You built layers of gravel, sand and soil in a clear jar, with a straw as a well, and poured in 'rain'.

items.p: What does each way of cleaning water do? Sort them.
items: settling
Removes bits you can see
a cloth filter
Removes bits you can see
boiling
Kills germs
chlorine
Kills germs
a sand filter
Removes bits you can see
strong sunlight on a clear bottle for 6 hours
Kills germs
items.a: see items
items.why: Settling and filters catch bits that are big enough to sink or get stuck. Boiling, chlorine and strong sunlight kill germs.

items.p: Boiling sea water makes it safe to drink.
items.why: False. Boiling kills germs, but the salt stays dissolved. If you boil sea water until it is all gone, the salt is left in the pot.

items.p: Why does a city with lots of roads and buildings often flood in heavy rain?
opts: Cities get more rain than villages
Rain cannot soak into cement and tar, so it all runs off at once
items.why: Hard ground has no gaps, so the rain runs off all at once and overfills the drains. Cities usually do not get more rain than villages. The difference is the ground, not the sky.

items.p: Match each water store to what it is.
pairs: a covered underground tank in the Thar desert
a deep well with stairs down to the water
a clay pot that keeps drinking water cool
a tank on a roof that sends water down the pipes
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These are ways Indian homes and villages store water, old and new.

items.p: A tap drips 50 millilitres in 10 minutes. One hour has 6 lots of 10 minutes. So in one hour it drips ____ millilitres.
items.why: 6 lots of 50 is 6 × 50 = 300 millilitres. That is more than a full tumbler of water every hour.
items.context: This question is about Drip Detective, where you caught a dripping tap's water in a cup for exactly 10 minutes.

items.p: Two neighbours share the same groundwater. One digs a much deeper borewell and pumps all day. What might happen?
opts: The other neighbour's shallow well may go dry
Nothing, because groundwater never runs out
items.why: The groundwater under the land is shared. Pumping a lot lowers the water level for everyone, so shallow wells dry first. Groundwater is not endless. It only refills as fast as rain soaks in.

items.p: Put the steps of a city water treatment plant in order.
items: Take water from a river or lake
Let it sit still so mud sinks
Pass it through sand and gravel
Add a tiny amount of chlorine
Pump it through pipes to homes
items.a: order shown
items.why: First the water is collected. Then heavy bits settle, smaller bits are filtered out, germs are killed with chlorine, and only then is it sent to homes.

items.p: Look at the chart from a Family Water Count. Which job used the most water?
items.why: Bathing has the tallest bar, at 150 litres. The toilet is second, at 120 litres. Picking drinking means guessing from what we think matters most, not reading the chart.
items.context: This question is about the Family Water Count. A family put a tally mark on a chart every time they used water for one day, then worked out the litres.

chart.title: Made-up example: one family's water in one day

items.p: In a village near Kolar, in Karnataka, the wells are drying up. Three people disagree about what to do.

views.who: Selvi, a farmer with a deep borewell
views.says: I need to pump every day to water my crops. If I stop, my family has no money.

views.who: Pushpa, whose old open well in the same village has gone dry
views.says: Deep borewells are taking the water we all share. Pumping should have a limit.
Pumping is fine only if it is no faster than rain refills the ground. Ponds and pits that catch rain help everyone.

items.ask: Pick the person you agree with most. Use what you saw in A Well in a Jar to back your choice. Then say what one of the others would say back.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and uses the jar well as evidence: pumping lowered the water for the whole jar, not just near the straw. It answers back fairly from another side, for example Selvi: a limit must still let farmers earn a living.
items.why: This is a real problem in many parts of India. Groundwater is shared, but each farmer needs it. There is no single right answer, so listen for evidence and fairness.
items.context: This question is about A Well in a Jar. You built layers of gravel, sand and soil in a clear jar, with a straw as a well, and poured in 'rain'.

items.p: Arjun's family boils their drinking water every morning. Then they keep it in an open bucket on the floor and dip a tumbler in to drink. By evening, is the water still safe? What would you tell him to change?
items.a: It may not be safe any more. Germs can get back in from dust, flies, and hands or tumblers dipped into the bucket. Keep the boiled water covered, up off the floor, and pour it out with a ladle or a tap instead of dipping in.
items.why: A strong answer sees that boiling only kills the germs that are there at that moment. Germs can come back in, so clean water must also be stored safely.

items.p: In the Invisible Ring, even the tap water left a faint ring on the dark plate. Does that mean the tap water is unsafe? Explain.
items.a: Not by itself. The ring shows that the tap water has some dissolved minerals, such as calcium. Small amounts of these are normal and harmless. The ring tells you something is dissolved, but not what it is or whether it is harmful. Only a proper test can tell that.
items.why: A strong answer separates 'something is dissolved' from 'something harmful is dissolved'. Almost all water has some minerals in it.
items.context: This question is about The Invisible Ring, where you dried spoonfuls of clear-looking water on a dark plate and looked at what was left.

items.p: Choose one job that uses lots of water in your home. Write two ways your family could use less for that job.
items.a: For example, bathing: use a bucket instead of a shower, and turn off the tap while soaping. Any two real ideas are good.
items.why: Small daily changes in the biggest water jobs save the most water. A strong answer picks a big job, not drinking.

items.p: Glass A is plain water. Glass B has salt dissolved in it. They look the same. How could you tell them apart without tasting?
opts: Dry a spoonful of each on a dark plate and see what is left
items.why: When the water evaporates, the dissolved salt is left behind as a white ring. Looking or smelling will not work, because dissolved salt is invisible and has no smell.
items.context: This question is about The Invisible Ring, where you dried spoonfuls of clear-looking water on a dark plate and looked at what was left.

items.p: A village well dried up after the forest on the hills above it was cut down. The hills became bare and hard. Why did the well dry up?
opts: The well was dug too deep
Rain ran off the bare hills before it could soak in and refill the groundwater
Trees drink all the rain, so cutting them should have helped
items.why: Forest floors slow rain down and let it soak in. Bare, hard ground makes it run away. So less water refilled the ground. Trees do use water, but forests help far more rain soak in than they use.

items.p: Water from a well has arsenic in it. A family boils it before drinking. Is it now safe?
opts: Yes, boiling makes all water safe
No. Boiling kills germs but does not remove arsenic.
Yes, if they boil it for an hour
items.why: Arsenic is dissolved, like salt. Boiling leaves it behind, and can even make it a little stronger as some water boils away. More boiling does not fix everything.

items.p: 1 millimetre of rain on 1 square metre of roof gives 1 litre of water. A roof is 50 square metres. 20 millimetres of rain falls on it. The roof can catch ____ litres.
items.why: Each square metre gives 20 litres, because 20 millimetres fell. 50 square metres give 50 × 20 = 1,000 litres. That is enough to fill about 66 buckets.
items.context: This question is about Catch the Rain, where you built a model house that catches rain from its roof.

items.p: Scientists measured the groundwater under north-west India using two satellites. What did the satellites actually measure?
opts: Tiny changes in the pull of gravity
items.why: Water is heavy, so it adds a tiny bit to the Earth's pull of gravity. When groundwater is pumped out, the pull gets slightly weaker, and the satellites feel it. Satellites cannot see under the ground. Groundwater is also not mostly in lakes.

items.p: Some of the water on Earth may be older than the Sun.
items.why: True, scientists think. A 2014 study worked out that up to half of Earth's water may have formed as ice in space before the Sun was born. It is a strong idea, but not yet proved.

items.p: Put these places in order, from the most rain in a year to the least.
items: Mawsynram, Meghalaya
Mumbai
Delhi
Jaisalmer, Thar desert
items.a: order shown
items.why: Mawsynram gets nearly 12 metres. Mumbai gets about 2 metres. Delhi gets about 80 centimetres. Jaisalmer gets about 20 centimetres.

items.p: Sohra, also called Cherrapunji, in Meghalaya, is one of the wettest places on Earth. Yet in winter many families there run short of drinking water. How can that be?
items.a: Almost all the rain falls in a few monsoon months. The hills are steep and much of the land is bare rock or thin soil, so the rain runs off fast instead of soaking in. Little is stored in tanks or in the ground. So in the dry winter months the springs and streams run low.
items.why: A strong answer says that how much rain falls matters less than whether it soaks in or is stored. It challenges the idea that lots of rain always means lots of water.

items.p: John Snow was a doctor in London in 1854. A widow called Susannah Eley lived in Hampstead, far away on a hill. She liked the water from the Broad Street pump, so it was carried to her house. She drank it and died of cholera. Nobody else near her was ill. Why was this strong evidence?
opts: She shared none of the Broad Street air, only its water, so the water must carry the illness
items.why: If cholera came from bad air, she should have been safe on the fresh hill. The one thing from Broad Street in her house was the water. 'She was old' does not explain why nobody else around her got ill.

items.p: A family boils all their drinking water. Which problems does boiling fix, and which does it not fix?
items: cholera germs
Boiling fixes it
arsenic from a deep well
Boiling does not fix it
germs from a dirty pond
Boiling fixes it
too much fluoride
Boiling does not fix it
salt from the sea
Boiling does not fix it
worm eggs
Boiling fixes it
items.a: see items
items.why: Boiling kills living things such as germs and worm eggs. It cannot remove things that are dissolved, such as arsenic, fluoride and salt. Those stay in the pot when water boils away.

items.p: A city must decide how people should pay for water.

views.who: Revathi, who runs a tea stall in Madurai
views.says: Water should be free. Nobody should go thirsty because they are poor.

views.who: An engineer at the city water board
views.says: If water is free, people waste it, and there is no money to fix the leaking pipes.

views.who: Jaya, a mother in a village that gets water by tanker
views.says: Give every family a little water free each day, and make people pay for more than that.

items.ask: Which idea do you agree with most? Give a reason. Then think of the poorest family in the city: what would happen to them under each idea?
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and gives a real reason, then looks at the poorest family under each idea. For example: free water helps the poor family but may leave the pipes leaking, so they might get dirty water. Paying for everything may leave them thirsty. Some Indian cities already give a little free water to every home and charge for more.
items.why: There is no single right answer. This is a real choice that cities make. Listen for reasons and for thinking about fairness.

items.p: A village pond is used by farmers, buffaloes, frogs, birds and children who swim. In a dry summer there isn't enough for everyone. Who should decide how it is shared, and how? Give reasons.
items.a: There is no single right answer. A strong answer names who should decide, such as the whole village together, and gives fair reasons. It remembers the animals and the people who cannot speak for themselves.
items.why: This is a real problem in many villages. Listen for reasons and fairness, not one answer.

items.p: Design a fair test to find out whether a matka cools water better in a breezy place or a still place. What will you keep the same? What will you change?
items.a: Use two matkas of the same size and clay, filled with the same water at the same time. Put one in a breeze and one in still air, both in the shade. Measure both after the same time. Change only the breeze.
items.why: A fair test changes only one thing. Everything else stays the same, so you know the breeze made the difference.

items.p: Draw the journey of one water molecule over a very long time. Show at least five places it has been, from space to your glass.
items.a: Any drawing with a sensible order, such as: ice in space, an icy comet or rock, the sea, a cloud, rain, a river, groundwater, a tree, a dinosaur, a well, your glass.
items.why: Water goes round and round for billions of years. It is never new and never used up.
items.art: A big empty swirl with a star at one end and a glass at the other.

items.p: In 2019, Chennai's main lakes nearly dried up. How did the city get water?
opts: Trains carried water from Jolarpettai, more than 200 kilometres away
It used sea water just as it was
items.why: Special trains carried millions of litres of water to Chennai every day. Sea water cannot be drunk until the salt is removed, which needs special plants and lots of electricity.

items.p: Many people say India is short of water mainly because it does not rain enough. Is that true?
items.why: False. India gets a lot of rain, but mostly in a few months. In many places more groundwater is pumped out than rain puts back, and rain on hard ground runs away to the sea. Saving and soaking in rain matters as much as how much falls.

experiments.title: Rain on Four Grounds: soak in or run off?
experiments.question: When rain falls on different ground, where does it go?
experiments.predict: Before you pour, guess. Put the four grounds in order, from the one that will soak up the water fastest to the one that will let it run away. Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, change only the ground. Use the same mug, filled to the same line. Pour from the same height, at the same slow speed. Time each one the same way.
results_table: Did the water soak in, run off or make a puddle?
Seconds until no puddle was left

materials.item: a mug, with a line marked on it
a bucket of water
four grounds: bare soil, grass, sand and cement or tiles. In a flat, use the soil of a big plant pot, a tray of sand, and a tile or steel plate, and skip the grass.
a clock or phone with a seconds timer

experiments.safety: Do this outside, on a balcony or in the bathroom, with a grown-up. Wet tiles are slippery, so walk carefully.

schedule.what: Pour the same mug of water on four grounds. Time how long each puddle lasts. Fill in the table.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw the four grounds, with arrows showing where the water went.
experiments.context: This is an experiment about what rain does when it lands. You pour the same mug of 'rain' on four kinds of ground, and watch where it goes.

flow.do: 1. Find four places close together: bare soil, grass, sand and a cement or tiled floor. In a flat, use a big plant pot's soil, a tray of sand and a tile. Do it on the balcony or in the bathroom. 2. Ask your child to guess which will soak up the water fastest, and why.
flow.say: Rain is about to fall on these four places. Which one do you think will drink it up fastest? Which one will let it run away?
flow.kid: Find four grounds: soil, grass, sand and cement. Guess! Which one drinks water fastest? Which one lets it run away?

ask.q: Why did you choose that one first?
good: Sand has gaps.
Soil is soft and spongy.

flow.context: This is the first step of Rain on Four Grounds. You find four kinds of ground and guess which one soaks up rain best.

flow.do: 1. Fill the mug to the line. 2. Hold it at knee height. 3. Pour it slowly onto the first ground. 4. Start the timer. 5. Stop it when no puddle is left. If water is still there after 5 minutes, write 'more than 5 minutes'. 6. Do the same on each ground.
flow.say: Pour slowly, like steady rain. Watch the water. Does it sink in, run away, or sit there?
flow.kid: Fill the mug to the line. Pour it slowly from knee height. Start the timer. Stop it when the puddle is gone. Do this on each ground.
flow.parent: Sand usually drinks water fastest. Then soil and grass. Cement and tiles let the water run off or sit in a puddle. That puddle will only go by evaporating, which takes much longer.

chart.title: Made-up example: how to fill in the table
cols: Soaked in, ran off or puddle?
rows: Ran off and made a puddle

flow.do: Look again at the cement puddle after 30 minutes, if you can.
flow.say: The cement puddle is smaller now. Nothing soaked in. So where did the water go?
flow.kid: Look at the cement puddle again later. Is it smaller? Where did the water go?

check.q: A puddle on cement slowly gets smaller. Where does its water go?
options: It evaporates into the air as invisible vapour
check.why: Cement has almost no gaps, so the water cannot soak in. Instead, it slowly turns into water vapour, an invisible gas, and goes into the air. Later, that vapour may become rain again. Picking 'soaks in' means thinking cement is like soil. Picking 'disappears' means thinking water can be destroyed. It can't. It only moves.

flow.do: Talk about the whole street, and the whole city.
flow.say: Imagine a whole city covered in cement and tar. Where does the monsoon rain go?
flow.kid: Imagine a whole city of cement. Where does all the rain go? What happens to the wells?
flow.think: Why do some cities flood in the monsoon, and then run short of water in summer?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: soft ground like sand and soil drinks rain, but cement makes it run off. What I saw: the sand puddle was gone in 10 seconds, but the cement puddle lasted more than 5 minutes. Why: sand and soil have tiny gaps for water to trickle into, and cement has none.

experiments.title: A Well in a Jar
experiments.question: How is water stored under the ground, and what happens to a well when we pump too fast?
experiments.predict: Guess first. When you pour 'rain' on top of the soil, where will it go? What will happen to the water at the bottom when you pump some out? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Pour the same amount of 'rain' each time. Pump the same number of times each time. Mark the water level after every change, so you can compare.
results_table: Water level at the bottom (cm from the bottom of the jar)

materials.item: a tall clear plastic jar or a big cut-off plastic bottle
small pebbles or gravel (from a plant shop or a building site), clean sand (plant shops sell both), and soil from a plant pot
a drinking straw, and a 10 ml syringe without a needle (any chemist sells one for a few rupees)
a jug of water and a cup
a marker pen and a ruler

experiments.safety: A grown-up cuts the bottle. Do not drink any of the water. Wash your hands after touching the soil.

schedule.what: Build the jar well. Pour rain, pump water out, and mark the level each time.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the jar with all its layers and the water level marks.
experiments.context: This is an experiment that builds a model of the ground under a village, in a clear jar. You can see how rain becomes groundwater, and how a well pulls it up.

flow.do: 1. Stand the straw against the inside wall of the jar, touching the bottom. 2. Hold it there. 3. Pour in gravel up to about 4 cm. 4. Add sand on top, then soil, until the jar is two-thirds full. 5. The straw is your well.
flow.say: This jar is the ground under a village, cut open so we can see inside. The gravel at the bottom is like rock with gaps. The straw is a well.
flow.kid: Stand the straw against the side of the jar. Fill with gravel, then sand, then soil. The straw is your well!
flow.context: This is the first step of A Well in a Jar. You build layers of ground in a clear jar, with a straw as the well.

flow.do: 1. Pour water slowly onto the soil, one cup at a time, like rain. 2. Watch through the side. Dry soil soaks up a lot first, so keep going. 3. Stop when water has collected between the pebbles at the bottom, about 3 to 4 cm deep. 4. Wait 2 minutes, then mark the water level with the marker. Write down how many cups it took.
flow.say: Watch closely. Where does the rain go? Can you see it in the gaps between the stones?
flow.kid: Pour water on top, one cup at a time, like rain. Watch through the side. Stop when water fills the pebbles at the bottom. Mark the level.

ask.q: Is the groundwater a lake or a pool?
good: No, it is in the gaps between the stones.
It fills the spaces, like water in a sponge.

flow.do: 1. Push the tip of the syringe into the top of the straw. Squeeze the straw tight round it with your fingers, so no air gets in. 2. Pull the plunger to suck water up, then squirt it into a cup. 3. Do this 10 times. 4. Mark the new water level.
flow.say: Now the village is pumping water from its well. Ten pumps. What happens to the water level?
flow.kid: Push the syringe onto the top of the straw. Pull to suck water up. Squirt it into a cup. Do it 10 times. Mark the new level.

check.q: In the jar well, the water level dropped after pumping. What would refill it?
options: More rain soaking down from the top
check.why: Groundwater only comes back when rain soaks down through the soil to refill the gaps. Pumping faster makes the level drop more. Covering the soil with plastic, like covering land with cement, stops rain soaking in. Picking 'pumping faster' usually means thinking a well makes its own water. It doesn't. It only collects water that soaked in.

flow.parent: Ten full syringes take out about 100 millilitres. In a jar about 10 cm across, that lowers the level by 2 to 4 cm, enough to see. With a small medicine dropper the change is too small, so use a syringe.

flow.do: 1. Pour half a cup of water on top. 2. Wait 5 minutes, then mark the level again. 3. Now cover the soil with a plastic bag, and pour another half cup on top of the plastic. 4. Wait 5 minutes and look at the level.
flow.say: First, a little rain. Then, what if the land were covered in cement? The plastic is our cement.
flow.kid: Pour half a cup of rain. Mark the level. Now cover the soil with plastic. Pour again. Does the well fill?
flow.think: In the real ground, rain can take months or years to reach a deep borewell. What happens if people pump faster than that?

rows: After half a cup more rain

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a well only stays full if rain soaks in to refill the ground. What I saw: the level fell from 4 cm to 2 cm after pumping. It came back to 3 cm after rain. It did not rise when the soil was covered. Why: groundwater sits in the gaps between stones, and only rain soaking down can refill those gaps.

experiments.title: The Cool Matka Test
experiments.question: Does water stay cooler in a clay matka than in a steel or plastic bottle? Why?
experiments.predict: Guess first. After four hours in the same place, which will be coolest: the matka, the steel bottle, or the steel bottle wrapped in a wet cloth? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, fill all three from the same tap at the same time. Keep them side by side in the same shady, airy place. Measure them all at the same time, with the same thermometer.
results_table: Is its outside dry or damp?

materials.item: a clay matka or a small unglazed clay pot
two steel or plastic bottles
a cotton cloth
a thermometer that can go in water

experiments.safety: Use tap water at room temperature, not hot water.

schedule.what: In the morning, fill the matka and two bottles, wrap one bottle in a wet cloth, and measure the start temperature.
Four hours later, measure all three again, feel the outsides, and fill in the table.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the matka and show, with arrows, where the water goes and where the heat goes.
experiments.context: This is an experiment that tests why water in a clay matka stays cool on a hot day, without a fridge.

flow.do: 1. In the morning, fill the matka and the two bottles from the same tap. 2. Wet the cloth, squeeze it a little, and wrap it round one bottle. 3. Put all three side by side in a shady, airy place. 4. Measure the water in each with the thermometer, and write it down.
flow.say: These three start the same. Same water, same tap, same place. Which do you think will be coolest by lunchtime?
flow.kid: Fill the matka and both bottles from the same tap. Wrap one bottle in a wet cloth. Put them side by side. Measure each one.
flow.parent: Wait about one minute before reading the thermometer, so it settles. If you have no thermometer, your child can dip a finger in each and put them in order from coolest to warmest. A small clay pot gives the fairest test, because a big matka holds more water and cools more slowly. A new matka works best after soaking it in water for a few hours. If the wrapped bottle ends up coolest, that is fine too: both cool by evaporation.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Cool Matka Test. You fill a matka and two bottles with the same water, so you can compare them later.

flow.do: 1. After about four hours, measure the water in each again. 2. Feel the outside of the matka and of the wrapped bottle.
flow.say: Feel the outside of the matka. Is it dry or damp? Where did that water come from?
flow.kid: Measure each one again. Now touch the outside of the matka. Is it damp? How did water get outside?

ask.q: Why is the outside of the matka damp?
good: Water seeped through tiny holes in the clay.
The clay is not completely waterproof.

chart.title: Made-up example results: water temperature after 4 hours in the shade
chart.note: These numbers are made up. All three started at 30 °C. Your numbers will be different, and a humid day will give smaller differences.

flow.do: Compare the three numbers. Then wet the back of your child's hand and blow on it.
flow.say: Feel your wet hand as I blow. It feels cold. That's the water evaporating and taking heat away. The matka does the same.
flow.kid: Wet the back of your hand. Blow on it. Does it feel cold? The matka works the same way!

check.q: Why does the matka keep water cooler than the steel bottle?
options: Water seeps out through the clay and evaporates, taking heat away
check.why: Clay has tiny holes. A little water seeps through and evaporates from the outside. Evaporating water carries heat away, so the water inside cools. The wet cloth does the same for the bottle. Picking 'clay is cold' is a common idea. But a dry clay pot left in the sun gets just as hot as anything else.

flow.do: Talk about the weather today.
flow.say: Was today dry or sticky? A matka cools best in dry, breezy air. Why might that be?
flow.kid: Is today dry or sticky? Matkas work best on dry, windy days. Why do you think?
flow.think: Your body has its own matka trick. What is it? (Hint: you do it when you run in the sun.)

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the matka keeps water coolest because water evaporates from its outside. What I saw: after four hours the matka was 24 °C, the wrapped bottle 26 °C and the steel bottle 29 °C. The matka felt damp outside. Why: evaporating water takes heat away with it.

experiments.title: The Invisible Ring: is clear water clean?
experiments.question: Can two glasses of water look exactly the same, but have different things hidden in them?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Two glasses of water look exactly the same. If you dry a spoonful of each on a plate, will they leave the same marks? And will plain tap water leave anything at all? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same amount of water from each glass, the same plate and the same sunny spot. Only the water changes.
results_table: How it looked in the glass
What it left on the plate when it dried

materials.item: three clear glasses
salt and a spoon
a little soil
a dark plate or a black plastic lid (a steel plate also works, but the ring is harder to see)
a sunny windowsill, or a place under a fan

experiments.safety: Do not taste or drink any of the test water. Wash your hands after touching the soil.

schedule.what: Mix the three glasses, let the muddy one settle, and put spoonfuls on the dark plate in the sun.
A few hours later, look at what each spoonful left behind.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the plate, showing what each spot left behind.
experiments.context: This experiment shows that water can hide things you cannot see. You dry spoonfuls of clear-looking water and look at what they leave behind.

flow.do: 1. Fill all three glasses with water from the kitchen tap. 2. Stir one big spoon of salt into glass B until it vanishes. 3. Stir one spoon of soil into glass C.
flow.say: Glass A is plain water. Glass B has salt in it. Can you still see the salt? Glass C has soil.
flow.kid: Fill three glasses from the kitchen tap. Stir salt into glass B. Stir soil into glass C. Can you still see the salt?

good: It dissolved.
It is still there, but in tiny bits we can't see.

flow.context: This is the first step of The Invisible Ring. You make three glasses of water: plain, salty and muddy.

flow.do: 1. Leave glass C still for 10 minutes. 2. Watch the soil sink to the bottom. 3. Hold glasses A and B up to the light side by side.
flow.say: The mud is settling, sinking to the bottom. Now look at A and B. Can you tell which one is salty, just by looking?
flow.kid: Leave the muddy glass still. Watch the mud sink. Now hold up A and B. Which is salty? Can you tell?

flow.wait: Leave the plate in the sun for 2 to 3 hours, or under a fan for about 4 hours.
flow.do: 1. Put one spoon of water from A on the plate. 2. Put one spoon from B a little way off. 3. Gently take one spoon from the clear top of C, and put it on too. 4. Leave the plate in strong sun, or under a fan, until the spots are dry.
flow.say: Now the water will evaporate. Whatever was hiding in it will be left behind.
flow.kid: Put a spoon from each glass on the dark plate. Keep the spots apart. Leave them in the sun to dry.

flow.do: Look closely at the three dry spots. Use a magnifying glass if you have one.
flow.say: What did each spot leave behind? Glass B looked perfectly clear. What was hiding in it?
flow.kid: Look at the dry spots. What is left? Glass B looked clear. What was hiding in it?

check.q: Glass A and glass B looked exactly the same. Glass B left a white ring when it dried. What does this show?
options: Water can look clear and still have things dissolved in it
check.why: The salt dissolved, so it spread out between the water molecules where you could not see it. When the water evaporated, the salt was left behind as a white ring. Plain tap water often leaves a very faint ring too. That ring is minerals the water dissolved from rock and soil on its way to you. Germs and poisons like arsenic are invisible in the same way. Picking 'salt turns into water' means thinking the salt was gone. It wasn't.

flow.parent: Plain water from a tap or borewell often leaves a faint white ring. These are minerals, such as calcium, that the water dissolved from rock and soil. That is normal. If your tap gives RO water, it leaves almost nothing, because RO takes most minerals out. The muddy water's top leaves a faint brown mark, because a little fine mud stays floating even after settling. If the plain water leaves nothing you can see, look with a magnifying glass, or try a spoon of borewell or bottled mineral water.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: water that looks clear can still have things hidden in it. What I saw: glasses A and B looked the same. But B left a thick white ring of salt, and A left only a faint mark. Why: the salt dissolved, so I could not see it until the water evaporated.

activities.title: Follow the Pipe

materials.item: a sheet of paper and coloured pencils
a phone, to ask a caretaker, plumber or panchayat office (optional)

activities.safety: Go up to the roof or terrace, or near a motor, only with a grown-up. Never touch electric motors or switches.

schedule.what: Follow the pipe from the kitchen tap back to the source. Draw it as a map.

activities.record: Draw a map of your water's journey. Start at the tap, and go back as far as you can. Add arrows. Then add where the used water goes.
activities.context: This activity traces the water in your home backwards, from the tap to wherever it really comes from. You draw the journey as a map.

flow.do: Stand at the kitchen tap with your child. Turn it on and fill a glass.
flow.say: Where does this water come from? The tap does not make it. It only lets out water that is already in the pipe. Let's find out what is behind the pipe.
flow.kid: Fill a glass at the kitchen tap. Where did this water come from? The tap does not make water. Let's follow the pipe back!

ask.q: Where do you think the water was this morning?
good: In the tank.
In the pipes.
In a river or a borewell.

flow.context: This is the first step of Follow the Pipe. You start at a tap and get ready to trace its water all the way back.

flow.do: 1. Follow the pipe as far as you can see it. 2. Look for an overhead tank on the roof, a sump underground, a motor, a water meter, a borewell or a handpump. 3. Your child draws each thing on the map, with arrows.
flow.say: Follow the pipe with your eyes. Where does it go into the wall? Where does it come out? Let's find the tank.
flow.kid: Follow the pipe. Where does it go? Look for a tank, a motor or a meter. Draw each one on your map, with arrows.
flow.parent: In a flat, look for the overhead tank on the roof and a sump at ground level. In a house, there may be a borewell with a motor. If you are not sure, ask the building caretaker or a plumber. In a village, the source may be a handpump, a well or a shared tap.

flow.do: Find out where the water gets into the tank or the pipe. Phone your caretaker, the plumber or the panchayat office together if you do not know.
flow.say: Now the hardest question. Where does the water come from before it reaches our tank?
flow.kid: Last question. Where does the water come from, before our tank? A river? A lake? A borewell? Ask a grown-up.

check.q: Water comes out of your kitchen tap. What is its real source?
options: A river, lake or reservoir, or groundwater pumped up from a borewell
check.why: The tap and the tank only hold and pass on water. They do not make any. The real source is a river, a lake or reservoir, or groundwater under the ground. All of these were filled by rain. Picking 'the tank makes it' means stopping the trail too early.

flow.do: Add where the water goes after you use it: the sink drain, the sewer, a soak pit or a septic tank.
flow.say: And after we use it? Where does it go when it goes down the drain?
flow.kid: Now add the other end. Where does the water go after you use it? Draw the drain.
flow.think: Is the water's journey a line from the river to the drain, or is it a circle?

activities.title: Rain Gauge and Sky Diary

materials.item: a clear plastic bottle with straight sides
scissors, used by a grown-up
a ruler, sticky tape and a few pebbles
a notebook for the sky diary

activities.safety: Only a grown-up cuts the bottle. Do not go out to read the gauge in a thunderstorm.

schedule.what: Make the rain gauge and place it outside. Start the sky diary.
Read the gauge at the same time. Draw the sky.
Read the gauge. Draw the sky.
Read the gauge. Draw the sky.
Read the gauge. Draw the sky.
Read the gauge. Draw the sky.
Read the gauge. Add up the week's rain and draw a line chart.

activities.record: Every day at the same time, write the date, the rain in millimetres, and draw the sky. At the end of the week, add up the total and draw a line chart.
activities.context: This is a week-long activity. You make a rain gauge, a tool that measures rain, and keep a diary of the sky, just like India's weather scientists.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up cuts the top third off the bottle. 2. Put pebbles in the bottom, and pour in water until it covers them. Mark that line as 0. 3. Tape the ruler on the side, with its 0 at the line. 4. Turn the top upside down and push it into the bottle as a funnel.
flow.say: Rain falls evenly, so this bottle catches the same depth of rain as the ground around it. We'll measure it in millimetres.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to cut the bottle. Put pebbles in. Add water up to a line, and call it 0. Tape on the ruler. Put the top in upside down.
flow.parent: The pebbles and starting water cover the bottle's curved bottom, so every millimetre on the ruler is a true millimetre of rain. Each small mark on a ruler is 1 millimetre. 10 millimetres make 1 centimetre.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Rain Gauge and Sky Diary. You make a rain gauge from a plastic bottle.

flow.do: Put the gauge in an open place with nothing above it. A terrace or a garden works. So does the outer edge of a balcony with no ledge over it. Weigh it down with stones, or tape it in place, so it does not blow over.
flow.say: Where should it go? Not under a tree or a roof, because they would block the rain or drip extra water in.
flow.kid: Put your rain gauge in an open place. Not under a tree. Not under a roof. Put stones around it.

flow.do: Every morning for a week, at the same time: 1. Read the water level against the ruler. 2. Write it in the sky diary, in millimetres. 3. Draw the sky. 4. Tip out water back down to the 0 line.
flow.say: Weather scientists all over India do exactly this, every morning at the same time. Today you are one of them.
flow.kid: Every morning, read your gauge. Write the number. Draw the sky. Then tip the water back to 0.

ask.q: Why do we read it at the same time every day?
good: So each reading is one whole day of rain.
To make it fair.

chart.title: Made-up example: rain in one week of the monsoon
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like.

flow.do: At the end of the week, add up all the readings. Draw a line chart of the seven days.
flow.say: How much rain fell this week altogether? Which day was the wettest?
flow.kid: Add up the whole week. Which day had the most rain? Draw a line chart.

check.q: Your rain gauge shows 0 millimetres, but the soil outside is wet. What is the best explanation?
options: Dew or a sprinkle wet the soil, but too little to measure, or the soil got water another way
The rain gauge made the rain disappear
check.why: A rain gauge only catches rain that falls into it. A tiny sprinkle, dew or a garden hose can wet soil without adding a whole millimetre. Picking 'soil makes its own water' means mixing up wet soil with a water source. Soil only holds water that came from somewhere else.

flow.think: If no rain falls this week, where can you find out how much fell in your city? (Look for the India Meteorological Department's rainfall report, or the newspaper.)

activities.title: The Family Water Count

materials.item: a 1-litre bottle
your usual mug, bucket and other water containers
a big sheet of paper for the tally chart, and a pencil tied to it

activities.safety: Do not climb up to look inside a toilet tank. Ask a grown-up, or read the size printed on it.

schedule.what: Measure how many litres your mug and bucket hold. Make the tally chart. Start counting.
After 24 hours, add up the litres. Draw a bar chart. Choose one way to use less.

activities.record: Fill in the tally chart for one whole day. Then multiply each tally by its litres, add up the total, and draw a bar chart.
activities.context: In this two-day activity your child counts how many litres of water the whole family uses in one day.

flow.do: Show the 1-litre bottle. Ask your child to guess how many of these the whole family uses in one day. Write the guess down and keep it.
flow.say: This bottle holds one litre. How many of these bottles of water do you think our family uses in a whole day?
flow.kid: This bottle holds 1 litre. Guess! How many bottles of water does your family use in a day? Write it down.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Family Water Count. You start by guessing how much water your family uses in a day.

flow.do: 1. Fill the mug from the 1-litre bottle. How much of the bottle does it take? 2. Fill the bucket with the bottle, counting the litres. 3. Find the toilet flush size. It is often printed on the tank, usually 6 to 10 litres.
flow.say: Before we count, we need to know how much each thing holds. Let's fill the bucket one litre at a time.
flow.kid: Fill the bucket with the 1-litre bottle. Count each bottle. How many litres does the bucket hold?

ask.q: Why do we measure the bucket first?
good: So we know how many litres one bucket is.
So we can multiply later.

flow.do: 1. Make a chart with rows: bathing, toilet, washing clothes, dishes and cooking, cleaning the floor, drinking. 2. Add columns: how many times, litres each time. 3. Stick it near the bathroom. 4. For 24 hours, everyone adds a tally mark each time they use water.
flow.say: You are the family's water auditor. For one whole day, everyone puts a mark here every time they use water.
flow.kid: You are the water auditor! Make the chart. Stick it up. For one day, everyone adds a mark each time they use water.

flow.do: 1. After 24 hours, multiply each row: times, multiplied by litres each time. 2. Add up all the rows. 3. Draw a bar chart, with one bar for each job.
flow.say: Let's find out the real number. Which job used the most water? How close was your guess?
flow.kid: Time to add up! Times multiplied by litres, for each row. Then add all the rows. Draw a bar for each job.

chart.title: Made-up example: one family's water in one day
chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your family's numbers will be different.

check.q: In the example chart, which job uses the least water?
check.why: Drinking has the shortest bar, only 10 litres for the whole family. Bathing and the toilet use far more. Picking bathing means reading the tallest bar instead of the shortest. Most of a home's water is for washing and flushing, not for drinking.

flow.do: Choose, together, one change the family will really make this week.
flow.say: Which job could we easily use less water for? What will we change?
flow.kid: Which job could use less water? Choose one change for your family. Write it on the chart.
flow.think: We used this many litres. A family in a desert village may manage on far less. How?

activities.title: Drip Detective

materials.item: a tap
a cup and a measuring cup or a teaspoon
a timer

activities.safety: Turn the tap off properly at the end.

schedule.what: Collect drips for 10 minutes. Measure them. Work out how much a dripping tap wastes in a day.

activities.record: Write how many millilitres dripped in 10 minutes. Then work out an hour, and a day.
activities.context: This activity measures how much water one dripping tap wastes, by catching its drips for exactly 10 minutes.

flow.do: Open a tap just enough that it drips, about one drop every second. Put a cup under it. Start a 10-minute timer.
flow.say: One drop is tiny. Surely a few drops don't matter? Let's find out.
flow.kid: Open the tap so it just drips. Put a cup under it. Start a 10-minute timer.
flow.context: This is the first step of Drip Detective. You make a tap drip into a cup for exactly 10 minutes.

flow.do: While you wait, count the drops in one minute together. Then do something else until the timer rings.
flow.say: Let's count the drops in one minute. Then guess how much will be in the cup after 10 minutes.
flow.kid: Count the drops for one minute. Now guess: how full will the cup be after 10 minutes?

flow.do: 1. Measure the water in the cup, using a measuring cup, or by counting teaspoons. One teaspoon is about 5 millilitres. 2. Work out one hour: 6 lots of 10 minutes.
flow.say: So that's how much in 10 minutes. An hour has 6 lots of 10 minutes. How much in an hour?
flow.kid: Measure the water. A teaspoon is about 5 millilitres. An hour is 6 lots of 10 minutes. How much in an hour?

check.q: A tap drips 50 millilitres in 10 minutes. How much does it drip in one hour?
check.why: One hour is 6 lots of 10 minutes. So it is 6 lots of 50 millilitres. 6 × 50 = 300 millilitres. Picking 60 means adding 10 instead of multiplying. Picking 500 means multiplying by 10, but an hour has only 6 lots of 10 minutes.

flow.think: That's in one hour. How much in a whole day of 24 hours? Who should fix a dripping tap at school, if nobody owns it?

activities.title: Read the Land like Varahamihira

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil
a hat and a water bottle

activities.safety: Go only with a grown-up. Never put your hand into a termite mound or a hole, and keep away from open wells.

schedule.what: Walk in a park, a field or a garden. Look for signs of hidden water. Record what you find.

activities.record: Draw a map of your walk. Mark every sign of hidden water you found, and say why you think it is a sign.
activities.context: If you have a park, a field or a garden nearby, try this walk. About 1,500 years ago, the scholar Varahamihira of Ujjain wrote about signs on the land that show where water hides underground. On this walk you look for signs like his.

flow.do: Before the walk, tell your child about Varahamihira.
flow.say: About 1,500 years ago, a scholar in Ujjain called Varahamihira wrote a huge book called the Brihat Samhita. One part tells well-diggers how to find water under the ground by reading the land. Let's try.
flow.kid: Long ago, a scholar called Varahamihira lived in Ujjain. He wrote about reading the land to find hidden water. Let's be land readers today!
flow.context: This is the first step of Read the Land. You hear about an old Indian scholar who found hidden water by reading signs on the land.

flow.do: Walk slowly. Look for plants that stay green when the plants around them are dry. Look for damp or dark soil, moss and termite mounds. Look for low places where puddles form after rain.
flow.say: Why would one tree be green when all the grass around them is brown? What might their roots have found?
flow.kid: Look for green plants in dry places. Look for damp soil and moss. Look for termite mounds. Mark each one on your map.
flow.parent: In the dry months the top soil dries out, and a shallow-rooted plant cannot reach water and turns brown. Trees such as neem, jamun and banyan send roots deep, down to damp soil, so they can keep their leaves green. Termites dry out easily, so they live where they can reach damp soil, and they build mounds from wet soil. Moss and dark soil mean water is near the surface. None of these signs is certain. Water could also come from a leaking pipe or a garden hose.

ask.q: Could a green plant in a dry place have another reason to be green?
good: Someone might water it.
There could be a leaking pipe.
Maybe this plant needs little water.

flow.do: Back home, look at the map together. Talk about how you could test one sign fairly.
flow.say: Varahamihira's signs often work, but not always. How could we test one sign properly, to see if it is true?
flow.kid: Look at your map. Pick one sign. How could you test it, to check if it is true?

check.q: A neem tree stays green in a dry field. What is the best way to test whether this is a sign of water?
options: Check many green trees and many dry places, and see where water is really found
Believe it, because an old book says so
Dig a hole under that one tree
check.why: One example can be a fluke. A fair test checks many trees and many places, and compares them. Digging under one tree tells you about one tree only. Picking 'an old book says so' means trusting who said it instead of checking. Even great scholars can be partly right.

activities.title: Carry the Morning's Water

materials.item: two 1-litre bottles of water
a path about 50 steps long, such as a corridor, a garden or a quiet lane

activities.safety: Carry only what feels comfortable. Walk, do not run. A grown-up comes along outdoors.

schedule.what: Count the litres used before breakfast, then carry water to feel what fetching water means.

activities.record: Write how many trips it would take to carry the morning's water, and how long one trip took.
activities.context: In many parts of the world, people still carry all their water home from a well, a pond or a handpump. In this activity you find out what that feels like.

flow.do: Count, or guess, how many litres your family used this morning before breakfast: brushing, the toilet, washing and the kettle.
flow.say: How much water did we use this morning, before breakfast? Let's count it in litres.
flow.kid: How much water did your family use this morning? Count it in litres. Brushing, toilet, washing, cooking.
flow.context: This is the first step of Carry the Morning's Water. You count how much water your family used before breakfast.

flow.do: 1. Your child carries the two 1-litre bottles to the end of the path, about 50 steps, and back. 2. Time the trip.
flow.say: Imagine there is no tap. Every litre we used this morning has to be carried from a well. Let's carry two litres there and back.
flow.kid: Carry 2 bottles to the end of the path and back. Time it. Now imagine there are no taps at all.

ask.q: How many trips would you need to carry the morning's water?
good: If we used 40 litres and I carry 2 each time, 20 trips.

flow.do: Talk about who carries water.
flow.say: In homes without a tap, women and girls do most of the carrying, sometimes for hours every day. Since 2019, India's Jal Jeevan Mission has been bringing taps to village homes. When water comes home, girls get more time for school and play.
flow.kid: In homes without taps, mostly women and girls carry the water. Sometimes for hours every day. How would your day change?

check.q: Why does a tap in every home matter so much for girls in many villages?

projects.title: Catch the Rain: a model rooftop tank

materials.item: a shoebox, or a small cardboard box
a piece of stiff card for the roof, and kitchen foil
a plastic bottle cut in half along its length, to be the gutter
a clean bottle for the 'tank', and a measuring cup
a watering can, or a bottle with holes in its cap
a clean bucket, for real rain on day 2

projects.safety: A grown-up cuts the bottles and card. On a rainy day, collect rain from a drainpipe only at ground level, never on a roof, and never in lightning.

schedule.what: Build the model house with a sloping foil roof and a gutter. Pour 'rain' and measure how much the tank catches.
On a rainy day, catch real rain from a drainpipe for 10 minutes and measure it. If it does not rain, wait for a rainy day.
Work out how much rain your real roof could catch. Draw a plan for your home.

projects.record: Write how much 'rain' you poured and how much the tank caught. Write how much real rain the bucket caught in 10 minutes. Draw your home's rain-catching plan.
projects.context: In this 3-day project, you build a model house that catches rain from its roof, like the tankas of the Thar desert and the rain tanks on many Indian roofs.

flow.do: 1. Cover the stiff card with foil. 2. Tape it onto the shoebox as a sloping roof. 3. Tape the half-bottle along the low edge as a gutter, sloping a little towards one corner. 4. Put the 'tank' bottle under that corner.
flow.say: In the Thar desert, families make every drop count. Rain on a clean roof or courtyard runs into a tank, and they drink it for months. Let's build one.
flow.kid: Cover the card with foil. Tape it on the box as a sloping roof. Tape the gutter along the low edge. Put the tank bottle under the corner.
flow.context: This is the first step of Catch the Rain. You build a model house with a roof and a gutter that leads rain into a tank.

flow.do: 1. Measure 500 millilitres of water in the measuring cup. 2. Pour it gently over the roof from the watering can, like rain. 3. Measure how much reached the tank.
flow.say: We poured 500 millilitres of rain. How much did the tank catch? Where did the rest go?
flow.kid: Measure 500 millilitres of water. Sprinkle it over the roof, like rain. How much reached the tank?

ask.q: Where did the rain that missed the tank go?
good: It splashed off the edge.
It dripped off the side of the gutter.
Some is still wet on the roof.

chart.title: Made-up example: model roof rain catch

flow.do: Improve the design. Try a steeper roof, a wider gutter, or a funnel at the tank. Pour 500 millilitres again.
flow.say: Engineers always try to do better. How could we catch more?
flow.kid: Can you catch more? Make the roof steeper, or the gutter wider. Try again with 500 millilitres.

flow.do: 1. On a rainy day, put a clean bucket under a drainpipe at ground level. 2. Collect for exactly 10 minutes. 3. Measure the water with a 1-litre bottle.
flow.say: This is real rain from our real roof. Let's see how much one drainpipe gives in ten minutes.
flow.kid: It's raining! Put a clean bucket under a drainpipe. Wait 10 minutes. Measure the water in litres.

flow.do: 1. Measure or estimate the area of your roof in square metres. 2. Use the rule: 1 millimetre of rain on 1 square metre gives 1 litre. 3. Draw a plan for catching rain at home.
flow.say: Here's a rule scientists use. One millimetre of rain on one square metre of roof gives one litre of water. Our roof is about this big. So how much could a rainy day give us?
flow.kid: Here is a rule. 1 millimetre of rain on 1 square metre makes 1 litre. How much could your roof catch? Draw a plan.

check.q: A roof is 50 square metres. 10 millimetres of rain fall on it. About how much water could it catch?
check.why: Each square metre catches 1 litre for every millimetre of rain. So each square metre catches 10 litres. 50 square metres catch 50 × 10 = 500 litres. That is more than 30 buckets. Picking 60 means adding 50 and 10 instead of multiplying.

flow.think: If every roof in your street caught rain, what would happen to the street's floods? And to its wells?

challenges.title: Cool Water Without a Fridge
challenges.problem: It is a hot day and the power is off. Keep a bottle of water as cool as you can for three hours, using no fridge, no ice and no electricity.
constraints: No fridge, no ice and no electricity.
Start with water from the same tap as a plain bottle, so you can compare.
Use only things you can find at home.
materials: two steel or plastic bottles of the same size
a thermometer, or your finger to compare
things from home, such as cloth, sand, a clay pot, a bowl, a fan made of card
general: Wrap the bottle in a wet cotton cloth, and keep the cloth wet.
Put it in the shade, where a breeze blows.
Use a clay matka or an unglazed clay pot.
creative: Make a pot-in-pot cooler. Put a small pot inside a bigger clay pot, and fill the gap with wet sand. A Nigerian teacher, Mohammed Bah Abba, made these popular in the 1990s to keep vegetables fresh in villages without electricity.
Stand the wrapped bottle in a shallow bowl of water, so the cloth keeps soaking water up.
Hang the wrapped bottle in a window where the wind blows through, like old desert coolers made of wet grass screens.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own cooler. Draw it, build it, and measure it against a plain bottle after three hours. Did yours win?
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. You must keep water cool on a hot day without any fridge or electricity, using the science of evaporation.

flow.do: 1. Fill two bottles from the same tap. 2. Measure both, or feel them. 3. One bottle stays plain. It is the 'control', the one you compare with.
flow.say: This plain bottle is our control. It shows what happens if we do nothing. Your cooler has to beat it.
flow.kid: Fill two bottles from the same tap. One stays plain. Your cooler must beat it!
flow.context: This is the first step of Cool Water Without a Fridge. You set up a plain bottle to compare your cooler against.

flow.do: List three ideas together before building anything.
flow.say: Remember the matka test. What made the matka cool? How can we use that trick?
flow.kid: Think like an engineer. Draw three ideas first. Remember what made the matka cool.

flow.do: Build the best idea. Put both bottles in the same place for three hours.
flow.say: Build it. Then we leave both bottles in the same place, so the test is fair.
flow.kid: Build your best idea. Put it next to the plain bottle. Wait 3 hours.
flow.parent: A wet cloth in a breeze usually works well, often several degrees cooler than the plain bottle. Wet sand between two clay pots works even better in dry weather. On a humid day, every cooler works less well.

flow.do: Measure both bottles. Read the usual solutions and creative ideas together. Then improve your design.
flow.say: Did your cooler win? By how many degrees? What could make it even better?
flow.kid: Measure both. Did your cooler win? By how much? Look at the other ideas. Can you beat them?

check.q: Which cooler will work best on a hot, dry, windy day?
options: A bottle wrapped in a wet cloth, in the shade and the breeze
A bottle wrapped in a dry wool blanket in the sun
A plain bottle in a closed cupboard
check.why: Wind and dry air make water evaporate fast. Evaporation takes heat away, so the wet cloth cools the bottle. Shade stops the sun heating it. Picking the blanket in the sun is a common idea, because blankets keep us warm in winter. A blanket slows heat moving in or out, but sunshine will still warm it, and it has no evaporation to cool it.

flow.think: People in hot, dry places have cooled water and homes this way for thousands of years. What else could we learn from them?

challenges.title: Water for a Desert Home
challenges.problem: A family lives in the Thar desert. About 20 centimetres of rain falls there in a whole year, mostly in a few big storms in July and August. The nearest well is 5 kilometres away, and its water is salty. Design a way for the family to have drinking water all year.
constraints: The family has very little money.
The water must stay clean for many months.
It must still work if the power goes off.
materials: a tray of sand, a small cup, foil and cling film, to build a model
general: Build a tanka: a covered underground tank, with a clean, sloping courtyard around it so rain runs in.
Catch rain from the roof with a gutter and a pipe into a tank.
Keep the tank covered and dark, so dirt, animals and sunlight stay out.
creative: A village pond, shared by everyone, with a fence to keep animals out of the drinking part.
Fog nets: in some dry hills near the sea, in Chile and Morocco, fine mesh nets catch drops from fog.
A johad, a curved earth wall, to slow rain so it soaks into the ground and refills the well. Remember: the well water here is salty, so this water is for animals and fields.
challenges.your_turn: Draw your design and label every part. How much rain must it catch to last a whole year? Build a model in a tray of sand and test it with a cup of 'rain'.
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You plan how a family in the Thar desert, where it rains on only a few days a year, can have clean water all year round.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Look at the rainfall chart in the 'Too little water' card.
flow.say: Mawsynram gets nearly 12 metres of rain. This desert family gets about 20 centimetres. And it comes all at once. How would you make it last a whole year?
flow.kid: This desert family gets very little rain. It comes in just a few storms. How can they have water all year?
flow.context: This is the first step of Water for a Desert Home. You read about a desert family's water problem.

flow.do: Work out the family's needs. Suppose 5 people each drink and cook with 5 litres a day.
flow.say: Five people, five litres each, every day. How much is that in a day? And in a whole year of 365 days?
flow.kid: 5 people use 5 litres each a day. How many litres a day? That's a lot for a whole year!

check.q: 5 people each use 5 litres of water a day for drinking and cooking. How much is that for the whole family each day?
check.why: 5 people, 5 litres each, is 5 lots of 5. 5 × 5 = 25 litres a day. Picking 10 means adding 5 and 5 instead of multiplying. For a whole year, 25 litres a day is more than 9,000 litres. So the tank must be big.

flow.do: 1. Draw a design and label it. 2. Build a model in the tray of sand. Sink a cup into the sand as the tank. Smooth foil around it as the sloping courtyard. 3. Pour a cup of 'rain' over it.
flow.say: Draw first, then build. Smooth the foil so it slopes towards the tank. Then let's make it rain.
flow.kid: Draw your design. Then build it in the sand tray. Sink a cup for the tank. Make a sloping foil courtyard. Pour some rain!

flow.do: Compare your design with the usual solutions and the creative ideas.
flow.say: Desert families have built tankas for hundreds of years. What did they know that we had to work out?
flow.kid: Desert families have done this for hundreds of years. How is your idea like a tanka? How is it different?
flow.think: If the courtyard is dirty when the rain comes, what happens to the drinking water for the whole year?

quiz.p: Which of these only stores water and passes it on, but is not where the water really comes from?
quiz.why: An overhead tank is filled by a motor from a sump, a borewell or a pipe. Rivers and groundwater are real sources, filled by rain.

opts: Rain held in tiny gaps between grains of soil and rock, like water in a sponge
A big underground lake under every city
Water lying in puddles on the ground
quiz.why: Groundwater fills tiny gaps, like water in a sponge. 'A big lake' is a very common picture, but it is mostly wrong. Puddles are on top of the ground, not in it.

quiz.p: Rain falls on four places. Where will it soak in fastest?
quiz.why: Sand has big gaps between its grains, so water rushes in. Cement, tin and tiles have no gaps, so rain runs off.

quiz.p: In the jar well, what made the water level at the bottom fall?
quiz.why: Pumping takes water out of the gaps, so the level falls. Only rain soaking down refills it.
quiz.context: This question is about A Well in a Jar. You built layers of gravel, sand and soil in a clear jar, with a straw as a well, and poured in 'rain'.

quiz.p: To keep water cool, why must a matka be plain clay, with no shiny coating?
opts: Water must seep through tiny holes in the clay and evaporate on the outside
A shiny coating makes the pot heavy
A shiny coating makes the water salty
quiz.why: The cooling comes from water evaporating on the outside of the pot. A shiny glaze blocks the tiny holes, so no water seeps out, and the pot stays as warm as a steel one.

quiz.p: What is a tanka, used in the Thar desert?
opts: A covered underground tank that stores rainwater
quiz.why: A tanka collects rain from a roof or a sloping yard and keeps it under the ground, covered, so it stays cool and clean for the dry months.

quiz.p: A glass of water is perfectly clear and tastes sweet. Is it safe to drink?
opts: Yes, clear water is always safe
Not for certain. It could carry germs or dissolved poisons that we cannot see.
quiz.why: Germs and dissolved substances like arsenic are invisible. The Broad Street pump in 1854 had clear, sweet water that spread cholera.

quiz.p: Muddy water was settled and poured through a cloth. It now looks clear. What should you do before drinking it?
opts: Boil it, or purify it, to kill germs
quiz.why: Settling and a cloth remove the mud you can see. Germs slip through. Boiling or a proper purifier kills them.

quiz.p: Why does muddy water come out clearer after it trickles through a thick layer of sand?
opts: The bits of mud get stuck in the tiny gaps between the sand grains, and the water slips through
The sand turns the mud into water
The sand kills all the germs
quiz.why: Sand grains have tiny gaps between them, like the ground that holds groundwater. Water fits through, but most bits of mud do not. A sand filter does not kill germs, so the water must still be boiled or purified.

quiz.p: Meenakshi counted her family's water on a Sunday, when everyone was home and all the clothes were washed. Why might one Sunday not show how much they usually use?
opts: Different days use different amounts, so it is better to count on a few days
Tally marks only work on school days
quiz.why: One day can be unusual. Counting on a few different days and comparing gives a fairer picture of what a family usually uses.

quiz.p: A shower uses about 10 litres of water each minute. Kavya's shower takes 8 minutes. A bucket bath uses one 15-litre bucket. How much water does the bucket bath save?
quiz.why: The shower uses 8 × 10 = 80 litres. The bucket uses 15 litres. 80 − 15 = 65 litres saved. Picking 80 means forgetting that the bucket bath uses some water too.

quiz.p: Why do wells and borewells in many parts of India go dry?
opts: People pump out groundwater faster than rain refills it
The water sinks too deep to be found
quiz.why: When pumping is faster than refilling, the water level falls. India pumps more groundwater than any other country. India gets a lot of rain, but unevenly.

quiz.p: In homes without a tap, who usually does most of the water-carrying?
quiz.why: Around the world, women and girls do most of the water-fetching in homes without water nearby. A tap at home gives them hours back every day.

quiz.p: Scientists think the hydrogen atoms in the water you drink were made…
opts: in the Big Bang, when the universe began
quiz.why: Hydrogen atoms were made in the Big Bang, about 13.8 billion years ago. The water itself goes round and round, so it is very old. 'Last monsoon' mixes up when the rain fell with when its atoms were made.

quiz.p: In 2009, data from India's Chandrayaan-1 Moon mission showed that…
opts: there is a trace of water in the Moon's dust
the Moon is made of ice
quiz.why: Chandrayaan-1 carried an instrument that found a thin trace of water in the Moon's dust. The Moon has no rivers, but its dark polar craters hold ice.

applications: City water treatment plants settle, filter and add chlorine to river water before it reaches our taps.
Overhead tanks use gravity to push water down to taps, even when the power is off.
Matkas and clay coolers keep water and food cool without electricity.
Rainwater harvesting: gutters and pipes lead roof rain into tanks or back into the ground.
Tankas, kunds, johads, ponds and stepwells have stored rain in India for centuries.
Water testing kits check wells for germs, arsenic and fluoride.
Desalination plants, such as those near Chennai, take salt out of sea water.
Farmers use drip irrigation, which gives each plant small drops at their roots, to save water.
Satellites that weigh water with gravity show where groundwater is being used up.
Doctors give oral rehydration solution, clean water with sugar and salt, to save people with diarrhoea.
Fire engines, hospitals and factories all need large stores of clean water.
Hydroelectric dams use falling water to make electricity.
Bleaching powder is added to village wells to kill germs, especially after floods.
Water meters measure how many litres each home uses.

open_questions.q: Where did Earth's water come from in the first place?
open_questions.why_open: Comets, asteroids and Earth's own rocks are all possible. The chemical fingerprints do not yet settle it.

open_questions.q: How much groundwater is under India, and how fast is it refilling?
open_questions.why_open: It is hidden, it moves slowly and it differs from village to village. Satellites and well records give only a rough picture.

open_questions.q: Can we predict a good or a poor monsoon months ahead?
open_questions.why_open: The monsoon depends on oceans, winds and land together, far away and nearby. Forecasts are getting better, but they are still often wrong.

open_questions.q: Why does arsenic come loose into some wells and not others nearby?
open_questions.why_open: Microbes, mud and pumping all seem to matter, but the mix is different in every place.

open_questions.q: Is there life in the hidden oceans of icy moons like Europa and Enceladus?
open_questions.why_open: They seem to have liquid water, and some of the chemicals life needs. Nobody has looked inside yet. Missions to Europa are on their way.

open_questions.q: How can we make clean drinking water cheap for everyone, without using lots of energy or wasting water?
open_questions.why_open: Boiling uses fuel, RO wastes water and removing salt from the sea uses lots of electricity. Scientists are testing new filters and materials.

open_questions.q: Could all life everywhere need liquid water, or could some life use something else?
open_questions.why_open: Every living thing we know needs water. But we have only ever studied life on one planet.
