maths.problem: A tap drips 50 millilitres in 10 minutes. How much does it drip in one hour? How much in one whole day of 24 hours? Give the day's answer in litres and millilitres.
maths.answer: 300 millilitres in one hour. 7,200 millilitres in a day, which is 7 litres and 200 millilitres.
maths.explain: One hour has 6 lots of 10 minutes. So in one hour the tap drips 6 × 50 = 300 millilitres. A day has 24 hours. 24 × 300 = 7,200 millilitres. 1,000 millilitres make 1 litre. So 7,000 millilitres is 7 litres, and 200 millilitres are left over. That is about half a bucket, from one small drip.
maths.context: This is about Drip Detective. You let a tap drip into a cup for exactly 10 minutes, then measured how much water was in the cup.

answer_chart.title: How much one dripping tap wastes, at 300 millilitres an hour

maths.why_maths: One drip looks too small to matter. Multiplying it by the hours in a day shows how tiny amounts add up to whole buckets.

maths.problem: Look at the family water chart. Bathing used 150 litres, the toilet 120, washing clothes 80, dishes and cooking 60, cleaning the floor 20 and drinking 10. How many litres did the family use altogether in the day?
maths.explain: Add the bars two at a time. 150 + 120 = 270. 80 + 60 = 140. 20 + 10 = 30. Then 270 + 140 = 410, and 410 + 30 = 440. So the family used 440 litres in one day.
maths.context: This is about the Family Water Count. A family put a tally mark on a chart every time they used water for a day. Then they worked out the litres for each job.

chart.title: Made-up example: one family's water in one day

maths.why_maths: A bar chart shows which job is biggest. Adding the bars tells you the whole day's water, so you can compare it with your guess and with other families.

maths.problem: A family of 4 used 440 litres of water in one day. If each person used the same amount, how many litres did each person use? Is that more or less than the 135 litres a day that city planners allow for each person?
maths.answer: 110 litres each. That is 25 litres less than 135 litres.
maths.explain: Share 440 litres equally among 4 people. 440 ÷ 4 = 110, because 4 × 110 = 440. So each person used 110 litres. 135 take away 110 is 25. So each person used 25 litres less than 135.
maths.context: This is about the Family Water Count, where a family worked out how many litres of water they used in one day.
maths.why_maths: A family's total depends on how many people live there. Sharing it out shows the litres for each person, so you can compare fairly with any family of any size.

maths.problem: A bucket holds 15 litres. One bucket bath uses one full bucket. A shower runs for 10 minutes and uses 6 litres every minute. Which uses more water, and by how much?
maths.answer: The shower uses more. It uses 60 litres, which is 45 litres more than the 15-litre bucket.
maths.explain: The shower runs for 10 minutes at 6 litres a minute. 10 × 6 = 60 litres. The bucket bath uses 15 litres. 60 take away 15 is 45. So the shower uses 45 litres more. That is 3 more whole buckets.
maths.context: In the Family Water Count, you measured how many litres your bucket holds, by filling it one litre at a time.
maths.why_maths: Comparing litres shows which habit uses more water. Then a family can choose the change that saves the most.

maths.problem: Look at the thermometer from the Cool Matka Test. Each big number is 10 degrees, and each small mark is 1 degree. What does it read? The water started at 30 °C. How many degrees did it cool?
maths.answer: It reads 24 °C. The water cooled by 6 degrees.
maths.explain: The liquid stops after the 20 mark, at the fourth small mark. Each small mark is 1 degree. So it reads 20 + 4 = 24 °C. The water started at 30 °C. 30 take away 24 is 6. So the matka cooled the water by 6 degrees.
maths.context: This is about the Cool Matka Test. You filled a clay matka with tap water, left it in the shade for 4 hours, and measured it with a thermometer.

chart.title: A thermometer in the matka water, in degrees Celsius (°C)

maths.problem: Riya, a girl in Class 3, did Rain on Four Grounds with more water. She poured 8 cups of water onto bare soil, one cup at a time. 6 cups soaked in. 2 cups ran off. What fraction of the water ran off?
maths.answer: 2 out of 8, which is the same as 1 quarter.
maths.explain: 2 cups out of 8 ran off. That is 2 eighths. Put the 8 cups into 4 equal groups of 2. One group ran off. So 2 eighths is the same as 1 quarter. The other 3 quarters soaked in.
maths.context: This is about Rain on Four Grounds, where you poured the same mug of 'rain' on different ground and watched whether it soaked in or ran off.

maths.why_maths: Fractions let you compare grounds fairly. Saying 'a quarter ran off' works whether you poured 8 cups or a whole monsoon.

maths.problem: Use the rain rule: 1 millimetre of rain on 1 square metre of roof gives 1 litre. A roof is 40 square metres. In one storm, 25 millimetres of rain fall. How many litres could the roof catch? How many 15-litre buckets is that, roughly?
maths.answer: 1,000 litres. That is more than 66 buckets.
maths.explain: Each square metre catches 25 litres, one for each millimetre. 40 square metres catch 40 × 25 litres. 40 × 25 = 1,000 litres. One bucket holds 15 litres. 15 × 66 = 990, so 1,000 litres is a little more than 66 buckets.
maths.context: This is about Catch the Rain, where you built a model house whose roof leads rain into a tank, then measured real rain from a drainpipe.
maths.why_maths: A storm feels like 'a lot of rain'. Multiplying turns it into litres, so a family can see how much their own roof could give them.

roots.context: We have been learning where our water comes from, how we store it and when it is safe. Now we ask what the water in our glass tells us about the world it came through.

deep_truth.truth: Plain tap water left a faint white ring when it dried. That ring is minerals, dissolved by the water from rock and soil on its way to you. Water picks up a little of every place it passes through. So each glass of water carries a trace of where it has been.
deep_truth.habit: We say 'plain water' or 'just water', as if water were empty. But almost no water on Earth is only water. It carries a little of the ground, the rock and the air it has passed through.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Invisible Ring, glass A and glass B looked the same, but B left a thick salt ring and plain tap water left a faint ring of minerals. Arsenic in Bengal tubewells came the same way, dissolved from the mud under the ground.

three.who_am_i: More than half of you is water. Your blood carries salts and food to every part of you, the way groundwater carries minerals from rock.
three.what_is_life: Every living thing we know needs water. Water carries food into a plant's roots and into every one of your cells.
three.what_is_this_world: Rain soaks through soil and rock, takes a little of them with it, and flows on to wells, rivers and the sea.

roots.thread: Rain is almost pure when it falls. As it soaks through soil and rock, it dissolves tiny amounts of them. Rivers carry these dissolved minerals to the sea, and over millions of years this helped make the sea salty. So the water in your glass, a well and the sea are joined by one journey, and each carries traces of the land it crossed.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka asks his son Shvetaketu to put salt in water overnight. In the morning the salt cannot be seen. But when Shvetaketu sips from the top, the middle and the bottom, the water tastes salty everywhere.
teachings.link: In the Invisible Ring, the salt in glass B could not be seen either. Drying the water showed that it was still there, spread all through the glass.

teachings.teaching: The best way to live is like water. Water helps all things and does not fight them. It flows to the low places that people look down on.
teachings.link: Water sinks into the ground, the lowest place, and that is exactly where it is stored and kept safe for wells and roots.

teachings.source: Thich Nhat Hanh, The Heart of Understanding (1988), on 'interbeing'
teachings.teaching: Look deeply at a sheet of paper and you can see a cloud in it. Without the cloud there is no rain, no tree, and no paper.
teachings.link: Look closely at a glass of water and you can find the rain, the rock it soaked through and the river or well it came from. The faint ring it leaves when it dries is part of that story.

science.text: Rivers carry minerals dissolved from rocks into the sea. Over millions of years, this is one main reason the sea is salty.
Scientists can often tell which rocks groundwater has passed through by testing the minerals dissolved in it.

other_view.view: Water itself is only H2O, two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. The minerals are other substances mixed into it, not part of the water. On this view, water carries things, but water itself keeps no record of where it has been.

practice.title: Taste the journey
practice.say: Pour a little of your drinking water into a steel glass. Take one small sip, and hold it in your mouth. Close your eyes. Does it taste of anything at all? Any taste comes from minerals it picked up from the ground. Think back along its journey: the tap, the pipe, the tank, a river or a well, the soil, and the rain. Now swallow slowly.

how_we_found_out.story: In the 1970s, many children in West Bengal and Bangladesh fell ill from germs in pond and river water. So governments and UNICEF, a United Nations group that helps children, paid for millions of tubewells. A tubewell is a narrow pipe pushed deep into the ground, with a handpump on top. Its water came from under the ground, away from the germs, and it was clear and cool. Fewer children got ill from germs. Nobody tested the water for anything else. In 1983, a skin doctor in Kolkata, K. C. Saha, saw patients with dark spots and hard, rough patches on their hands and feet. He traced the cause to arsenic, a poison, in their tubewell water. The arsenic had dissolved from the mud under the ground. Later, Dipankar Chakraborti and his team at Jadavpur University tested tens of thousands of wells. Today, wells in many villages are tested and painted green if safe and red if not.
how_we_found_out.who: K. C. Saha, a skin doctor in Kolkata, and Dipankar Chakraborti of Jadavpur University
how_we_found_out.when: 1983, and the years of testing after it
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Clear water from under the ground, away from the germs, must be safe to drink. Patients' skin, and then tests on the wells, showed that it can carry arsenic dissolved from the rocks.
